body:
Claude Code is Anthropic's terminal-based coding agent. This guide walks through a first install end to end: pick an install method, authenticate, and confirm the CLI is healthy before you point it at real work.

 This is an original walkthrough. Command flags and supported platforms change; the official setup documentation is always the authoritative list. 

Before you start

You need a terminal, a project directory to work in, and a Claude account (a Claude Pro or Max subscription, or an API-billing account on the Claude Console).

If you plan to install through npm, you also need Node.js 18 or newer. Check what you have:

bash
`node --version npm --version`

If Node is missing or older, install a current LTS release from nodejs.org first — the npm install method will fail on unsupported versions.

Choose an install method

There are two supported paths. Pick one; installing both leaves two binaries on your PATH and makes upgrades confusing.

**Native installer** — the shortest path, no Node.js required. On macOS and Linux:

bash
`curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash`

On Windows, run PowerShell and use the equivalent installer script documented on the official setup page.

**npm** — preferable if you already manage developer tooling with npm and want upgrades in the same place as the rest of your global packages:

bash
`npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`

Do not install with `sudo`. A global npm install that needs root usually means your npm prefix points at a system directory; fixing the prefix is safer than escalating privileges for every upgrade.

Verify the install

Open a new terminal so PATH changes take effect, then:

bash
`claude --version`

If the shell reports "command not found", the install directory is not on your PATH. The installer prints the directory it used — add it to your shell profile (`~/.zshrc`, `~/.bashrc`, or your PowerShell profile) and reopen the terminal.

Authenticate

Change into a project directory and start Claude Code:

bash
`cd path/to/your/project claude`

On first run it walks you through login in the browser. Subscription accounts sign in with their Claude credentials; API-billing accounts authenticate against the Console. Credentials are stored per machine, so you authenticate once per workstation, not once per project.

To check or change accounts later, use the `/login` and `/status` commands inside a session.

Confirm everything is healthy

Claude Code ships a self-check that reports install method, version, and PATH problems:

bash
`claude doctor`

Run it whenever the CLI behaves oddly after an OS or Node upgrade — it catches the common "two installs on PATH" case that produces confusing version mismatches.

First run

Start in a directory that is already a git repository. Claude Code reads the working tree, and having git history available means you can review and revert anything it proposes.

Ask it something small and verifiable first, for example a summary of the project structure. Confirm you get a sensible answer before handing it a real task.

Keeping it up to date

The native install updates itself; npm installs upgrade with:

bash
`npm update -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`

Where to go next

- Set up your Claude API key — for

working with the API directly rather than through the CLI.

- Official Claude Code documentation

— full command, configuration, and permission reference.

frontmatter.title: Your First Conversation with the Claude API
frontmatter.description: Send your first Messages request, read the response shape, and carry a multi-turn conversation.

body:
Learning objectives
- →Call the Messages API with a system prompt and one user turn
- →Read content, usage, and stop_reason from the response
- →Carry conversation state across turns yourself, since the API is stateless

Overview

Almost everything you build on Claude goes through one endpoint: `POST /v1/messages`. Tool use, vision, streaming, and structured output are all options on that single call. Learn its shape once and the rest is configuration.

A request has three required parts — a `model`, a `max_tokens` ceiling, and a `messages` array — plus an optional `system` prompt that sets standing instructions.

python
`import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic() response = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024, system="You are a concise technical writer. Answer in at most three sentences.", messages=[ {"role": "user", "content": "What is an idempotent HTTP method?"}, ], ) print(response.content[0].text)`

Reading the response

The response is an object, not a string. Four fields carry most of what you need:

FieldWhat it holds
`content`A list of content blocks. Text lives in blocks of `type: "text"`.
`stop_reason`Why generation stopped — `end_turn`, `max_tokens`, `tool_use`, `refusal`.
`usage`Input and output token counts, for cost and budgeting.
`model`The model that actually served the request.

python
`print(response.stop_reason) # "end_turn" print(response.usage.input_tokens, response.usage.output_tokens)`

Always check `stop_reason` before trusting the text. `end_turn` means Claude finished on its own. `max_tokens` means you cut it off mid-answer — raise the ceiling and try again.

Iterate `content` rather than indexing block zero once your requests involve thinking or tools, since the first block may not be the text you want:

python
`text = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")`

The API is stateless

There is no conversation ID and no server-side history. Every request carries the entire conversation, and you own that array. Continuing a conversation means appending the assistant's reply and the next user message, then sending the whole thing again.

Examples

**A two-turn conversation**

python
`messages = [{"role": "user", "content": "My name is Layla."}] first = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=messages ) messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": first.content}) messages.append({"role": "user", "content": "What is my name?"}) second = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=1024, messages=messages ) print(second.content[0].text) # refers back to "Layla"`

Append `first.content` — the whole block list — not just the extracted string. Preserving the original blocks is what keeps later features (thinking, tool calls) working unchanged.

**The same call in TypeScript**

typescript
`import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk"; const client = new Anthropic(); const response = await client.messages.create({ model: "claude-opus-5", max_tokens: 1024, messages: [{ role: "user", content: "What is an idempotent HTTP method?" }], }); for (const block of response.content) { if (block.type === "text") console.log(block.text); }`

**Streaming, for anything a user watches**

python
`with client.messages.stream( model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=4096, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Explain HTTP caching."}], ) as stream: for text in stream.text_stream: print(text, end="", flush=True) final = stream.get_final_message()`

Streaming shows tokens as they arrive and avoids request timeouts on long responses.

Best Practices

- **Put standing instructions in `system`, not in the user turn.** Role, tone, and output

format belong there; the user turn is the actual request.

- **Set `max_tokens` generously.** It is a ceiling, not a target — you are billed for tokens

produced, not for the cap. Roughly 16k is a sane default for non-streaming calls; go higher when streaming.

- **Stream anything a human waits on.** It improves perceived latency and sidesteps timeouts

on long generations.

- **Append the full `content` list** when continuing a conversation, not a flattened string.
- **Track `usage` from day one.** Token counts are the only honest basis for cost estimates,

and they are right there in every response.

Common Mistakes

- **Reading `response.content[0].text` unconditionally.** It works for plain text today and

breaks the moment a non-text block comes first. Filter by block type instead.

- **Expecting the API to remember.** Without resending the history, every call starts from

nothing.

- **Starting the array with an `assistant` message.** The first message must be `user`.
- **Ignoring `stop_reason`.** A truncated answer looks like a complete one until you check.
- **Setting `max_tokens` to something tiny to save money.** It truncates answers and costs

you a retry; billing follows tokens generated, not the ceiling.

- **Inventing model IDs.** Use the exact string from the model overview — a near-miss like

`claude-opus-5.0` returns a `404`.

Official resources
- Messages API reference
- Model overview and IDs

frontmatter.title: Set Up Your Claude API Key
frontmatter.description: Create an API key, store it safely as an environment variable, and confirm the SDK can read it.

body:
Learning objectives
- →Create an API key in the Claude Console and understand what it grants access to
- →Store the key as an environment variable instead of hardcoding it
- →Verify the official SDK picks the key up with a single call

Overview

Every request to the Claude API is authenticated with an API key. Before you write a single line of application code, you need a key that exists, is funded, and is readable by your program without being written into your source.

This lesson covers the three steps in order: create the key, store it, prove it works.

An API key is a bearer credential — anyone holding it can spend on your account. Treat it like a password, not like a username.

 API billing is separate from a Claude.ai subscription. A Pro or Max plan does not include API credits; you fund API usage in the Console. 

Step 1 — Create the key

- Sign in to the Claude Console.
- Add a payment method and some initial credit under **Billing** if you have not already.
- Open **Settings → API keys** and create a new key.
- Give it a name that says where it will be used (`laptop-dev`, `ci-staging`) so you can

revoke exactly the right one later.

The key is shown once. Copy it now; if you lose it, delete it and create another rather than hunting for a way to view it again.

Step 2 — Store it as an environment variable

The official SDKs read `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` from the environment automatically. Set it in your shell profile, not in your project files:

bash
`# macOS / Linux — add to ~/.zshrc or ~/.bashrc export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="sk-ant-..."`

powershell
`# Windows PowerShell — persists for your user account setx ANTHROPIC_API_KEY "sk-ant-..."`

Open a new terminal afterwards so the variable is actually in the environment.

For project-local configuration, a `.env` file loaded by your language's dotenv library works too — as long as `.env` is listed in `.gitignore`.

Step 3 — Verify

Install the SDK and make one small call.

<CodeGroup>

bash
`pip install anthropic`

bash
`npm install @anthropic-ai/sdk`

</CodeGroup>

python
`import anthropic client = anthropic.Anthropic() # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment response = client.messages.create( model="claude-opus-5", max_tokens=64, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with the single word: ready"}], ) print(response.content[0].text)`

If this prints `ready`, your key is valid and your environment is wired correctly. A `401` means the key is wrong or missing; a `400` means the request body is malformed, which at this size usually means a typo in the model name.

Examples

**Checking the variable is visible to your shell**

bash
`# macOS / Linux echo "${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY:0:10}..."`

Printing a prefix confirms the variable exists without dumping the whole secret into your terminal history.

**Passing the key explicitly** — useful when one process talks to two accounts:

python
`client = anthropic.Anthropic(api_key=os.environ["WORK_ANTHROPIC_KEY"])`

Read it from an environment variable even here. The point is not "never write `api_key=`", it is "never write the literal key".

**Separate keys per environment**

Key nameUsed byRevoke when
`laptop-dev`your machinelaptop is lost or you leave the project
`ci-staging`CI pipelinepipeline is retired
`prod-api`production servicerotated on schedule

Best Practices

- **One key per environment.** Shared keys cannot be revoked without breaking everything at

once.

- **Never commit a key.** Add `.env` to `.gitignore` before creating it, not after.
- **Rotate on exposure, immediately.** If a key reaches a screenshot, a log, a pull request,

or a chat message, delete it in the Console. Rotation is cheap; an unknown-exposure key is not.

- **Set a spend limit** in the Console while you are learning. It converts a runaway loop

from a bill into an error message.

- **Keep keys out of client-side code.** Anything shipped to a browser or mobile app is

readable by users. Calls to Claude belong on a server you control.

Common Mistakes

- **Hardcoding the key** in a source file "just for now". It reaches version control on the

next commit and stays in history even after you delete the line.

- **Setting the variable in one terminal only.** `export` applies to the current shell

session. Add it to your profile, then open a new terminal.

- **Expecting a Claude.ai subscription to cover API calls.** They are separate products with

separate billing; API calls need Console credit.

- **Committing `.env`.** Check with `git status` before your first commit — once it is in

history, rotating the key is the only real fix.

- **Pasting a key into a chat or an issue to ask for help.** Redact it; anyone reading the

thread can spend it.

Next: your first API conversation.

Official resources
- Claude Console — API keys
- Claude API documentation

body:
Learn more
Repository
https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python

Docs
https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk

Overview

The Agent SDK exposes Claude Code's **agent loop as a library**. The docs are specific that it gives you the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code, so the harness behaviour you get interactively is the harness behaviour you embed. It ships built-in tools for reading files, running commands and editing code, so an agent can start working without you implementing tool execution yourself.

For other languages, the docs point to running the CLI programmatically with `-p` and `--output-format json` rather than a native SDK. For the design thinking behind the harness, the docs link the "A harness for every task" post.

Installation

**TypeScript:**

bash
`npm init -y npm pkg set type=module npm install @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk npm install --save-dev tsx`

Setting `type: module` lets your agent script use top-level `await`; `tsx` runs TypeScript directly. In an existing CommonJS project, skip the module change and name the script `agent.mts` instead.

**Python (uv):**

bash
`uv init uv add claude-agent-sdk`

**Python (pip):**

bash
`python3 -m venv .venv source .venv/bin/activate pip install claude-agent-sdk`

Using a virtual environment avoids the externally-managed-environment error recent Debian, Ubuntu and Homebrew Python installs return for a global pip install.

Configuration

Configuration centres on `ClaudeAgentOptions` (Python) or the options object (TypeScript). The options you set control the harness: which tools the agent may use, the system prompt, permissions and context handling.

The `allowed_tools` list is the permission boundary. Setting it explicitly is how you keep a production agent from doing more than intended.

Examples

**Python:**

python
`import asyncio from claude_agent_sdk import query, ClaudeAgentOptions async def main(): async for message in query( prompt="Find and fix the bug in auth.py", options=ClaudeAgentOptions(allowed_tools=["Read", "Edit", "Bash"]), ): print(message) asyncio.run(main())`

**TypeScript:**

typescript
`import { query } from "@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk"; for await (const message of query({ prompt: "Find and fix the bug in auth.ts", options: { allowedTools: ["Read", "Edit", "Bash"] } })) { console.log(message); }`

Both stream messages as the agent works - Claude reads the file, finds the bug and edits it, and your program consumes the messages as they arrive.

Best Practices

- **Set allowed_tools explicitly.** It is the permission boundary for a production agent.
- **Stream rather than buffer** - the async iteration surfaces progress and lets you act

mid-run.

- **Use the Python SDK packages; use `claude -p` for other languages.** The docs route

non-Python/TypeScript callers to the CLI with JSON output.

- **Choose the SDK over the CLI when you need structured control** - structured outputs,

tool-approval callbacks and native message objects are SDK features.

- **Keep secrets out of the prompt.** The agent's context is where injected instructions land.

FAQ

**How is this different from the CLI?** The CLI is a process boundary - text in, exit code out. The SDK is an in-process library with structured message objects and callbacks for tool approval.

**Is it the same agent as Claude Code?** Yes - the docs state it provides the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code.

**Does it support other languages?** Python and TypeScript have packages. For other languages the docs suggest running the CLI programmatically with `-p --output-format json`.

**What does the SDK give me that the CLI does not?** Structured outputs, tool-approval callbacks and native message objects, per the docs.

- Repository↗
- Documentation↗

body:
Learn more
Repository
https://github.com/anthropics/skills

Docs
https://github.com/anthropics/skills/blob/main/README.md

Overview

Anthropic's public repository of **reference skills** - folders of instructions, scripts and resources that Claude loads dynamically to improve performance on specialised tasks. The README frames the purpose precisely: skills teach Claude how to complete specific tasks in a repeatable way, whether that is producing documents to the company's brand guidelines, running an analysis through the organisation's own workflow, or automating a personal routine.

Each skill is self-contained in its own folder with a `SKILL.md` file carrying the instructions and metadata Claude uses. The collection spans creative applications, technical tasks (testing web apps, MCP server generation) and enterprise workflows. The document skills under `skills/docx`, `skills/pdf`, `skills/pptx` and `skills/xlsx` are the ones powering Claude's document capabilities in production - released as source-available reference rather than open source.

This repository also carries the Agent Skills **specification** in `./spec` and a **template** in `./template`, and the README notes the skills follow an open standard that works across multiple AI tools.

Installation

Claude Code users can register the repository as a marketplace or copy individual skills into their own skills directory. The skills are also usable from Claude.ai and the API, because they follow the open standard rather than a single host's format.

Per the README, the repository can be registered as a Claude marketplace so the skills appear alongside built-ins; the individual skill folders under `skills/` can also be copied directly.

Configuration

Each skill is configured through its own `SKILL.md` frontmatter - the metadata that governs when Claude loads it and how it is invoked. The `template/` folder in the repository is the starting point for authoring your own.

Claude Code extends the standard with additional features such as invocation control, subagent execution and dynamic context injection, so a skill written for the standard works in more than one host.

Examples

- **Browse by category.** `./skills` is organised into Creative & Design, Development &

Technical, Enterprise & Communication, and Document skills.

- **Copy one pattern, not the repo.** Each folder is self-contained, so lifting a single

skill into your own repository is the intended reuse path.

- **Use the docx/pdf/pptx/xlsx skills as the complex example.** They are the production

document skills, included as a reference for how a non-trivial skill is structured.

Best Practices

- **Read a skill before copying it.** The README is explicit that implementations and

behaviours may differ from what the skill shows, and that you should test thoroughly in your own environment before relying on it for critical tasks.

- **Start from the template** when authoring, so your skill matches the standard's frontmatter

conventions.

- **Keep skills scoped to one repeatable task.** The definition is a repeatable task, not a

general capability.

- **Note the licence split** - many skills are Apache 2.0 open source, while the document skills

are source-available; check before shipping.

FAQ

**What is the difference between this and the Agent Skills standard?** This repository is Anthropic's *implementation* and examples; the standard itself lives in the `./spec` folder and at agentskills.io.

**Are these production-ready?** They are described as demonstration and educational in the README's disclaimer - useful patterns and reference implementations, but test in your own environment before relying on them for critical tasks.

**Can I use these with tools other than Claude Code?** The skills follow the Agent Skills open standard, which is designed to work across multiple AI tools; Claude Code adds extensions on top.

**What is the licence?** Many skills are Apache 2.0. The document skills (docx, pdf, pptx, xlsx) are source-available rather than open source.

body:
Learn more
Repository
https://github.com/wshobson/agents

Docs
https://github.com/wshobson/agents/blob/main/README.md

Overview

A large community marketplace of agentic building blocks - the README advertises 94 plugins, 202 agents, 184 skills and 105 commands - with an unusual architecture: **one source of truth (`plugins/`) and six target harnesses**. The project's stated goal is that each harness gets its own idiomatic, harness-native artefacts rather than lowest-common-denominator translations, with the capability matrix documented in `docs/harnesses.md`.

It is built for Claude Code and consumed natively by Codex CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, the Antigravity CLI, GitHub Copilot and Pi. For a reader mapping this onto the rest of the glossary: the **plugin** is the installable packaging unit, while the skills and agents inside are what actually extend the agent.

Installation

**Claude Code** - add the marketplace, then install a plugin:

bash
`/plugin marketplace add wshobson/agents /plugin install python-development`

**Codex CLI** installs natively from the committed registries (which point at the source `plugins/`):

bash
`npx codex-marketplace add wshobson/agents`

**Cursor** adds the marketplace, then installs with `/plugin install <name>`.

**Antigravity, OpenCode and Pi** use clone + generate (the transformed trees are gitignored):

bash
`gh repo clone wshobson/agents ~/agents && cd ~/agents make generate HARNESS=antigravity && make install-antigravity make install-opencode`

**Skills only** - the Agent Skills installers read `plugins/*/skills/` straight from GitHub, with no clone and no generate step (skills only, no agents or commands):

bash
`gh skill install wshobson/agents npx skills add wshobson/agents --skill python-testing-patterns`

Configuration

Configuration is per-harness and mostly lives in `docs/harnesses.md`, which carries the capability matrix and per-harness gotchas. The `make generate HARNESS=<name>` step is the mechanism for clone-based harnesses - it transforms the canonical `plugins/` tree into each harness's native layout.

Examples

- **Pick one plugin for one need** - the plugins are granular, single-purpose installable units,

so install narrowly rather than the whole marketplace.

- **Skills without the plugin machinery** - use the Agent Skills installers when you only want

instructions and not agents, commands or hooks.

- **Cross-harness consistency** - if you run two different coding agents on the same repo, this

is the case for a single source generating both.

Best Practices

- **Install narrowly.** 94 plugins is a menu, not a bundle; take the one you need.
- **Read the harness matrix first.** Feature parity across six harnesses is not automatic -

the capability matrix tells you what you lose on a given agent.

- **Use the skills-only path when that is all you want** - it skips clone and generate entirely.
- **Review community content as you would any third-party dependency** - it is contributed code

running with your permissions.

FAQ

**Is it really six harnesses from one source?** Yes - the README states one source of truth (`plugins/`) with six target harnesses, each getting harness-native artefacts.

**What is the difference between a plugin and a skill here?** A plugin is the installable unit; the skills inside it are the packaged instructions. You can install skills alone.

**Does it work with Cursor?** Yes - add the marketplace, then `/plugin install <name>`.

**Are the clone-based harnesses hard to set up?** Antigravity, OpenCode and Pi need a clone and a generate step (`make generate HARNESS=<name>`); the generated trees are gitignored.

body:
Learn more
Repository
https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-action

Docs
https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code-action/blob/main/README.md

Overview

Claude Code Action is a general-purpose GitHub Action for pull requests and issues. It detects when to activate based on your workflow context - whether that is responding to an @claude mention, being assigned an issue, or an automation step with an explicit prompt - and runs Claude Code with access to GitHub APIs and file operations on your runner.

Capabilities per the README include answering questions about code and architecture, analysing PR changes and suggesting improvements, implementing fixes, refactors and features, progress tracking with live-updating checkboxes, and structured outputs that become GitHub Action outputs for complex automations. It supports multiple authentication methods: Anthropic direct API (API key or workload identity federation), Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry. The action runs entirely on your own GitHub runner - only the model call goes to your chosen provider.

Installation

The quickest path is from Claude Code itself:

bash
`claude`

Then run:

text
`/install-github-app`

That walks you through creating the GitHub app and adding the required secrets. You must be a repository admin to install the app and add secrets, and this quickstart only applies to direct Anthropic API users. For AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI or Microsoft Foundry, follow the cloud-providers documentation instead.

A basic workflow reference:

yaml
`- uses: anthropics/claude-code-action@v1 with: prompt: "Review this PR for correctness and security issues" claude_args: "--allowedTools 'Read,Grep,Glob'"`

Configuration

Two inputs carry the configuration:

- **`prompt`** - the instruction for this run.
- **`claude_args`** - flags passed to Claude Code, the key place to constrain tools.

Tool access is where the permissions decision lives. Keep the allowed-tools list tight for a review job; a reviewer that can write is a reviewer that can push changes you did not ask for.

If you are upgrading from v0.x, the migration guide covers the configuration simplification in v1.0 while retaining compatibility with most existing setups.

Examples

**Automatic PR review** - trigger on pull requests and have Claude report correctness and security findings.

**Path-specific review** - run only when critical files change, so the action is not invoked on every documentation typo.

**External contributor review** - special handling for first-time contributors, where extra scrutiny is warranted.

**Automation with structured output** - request JSON results that become typed action outputs for a downstream step.

Best Practices

- **Constrain the tools.** Set `claude_args` with an explicit allowed-tools list; the default

is broader than a CI job needs.

- **Scope triggers deliberately.** Path-specific triggers keep the action off unrelated PRs.
- **Choose the auth path that fits your infra** - workload identity federation avoids long-lived

keys, while cloud providers keep the model call inside your own cloud boundary.

- **Treat it as a reviewer, not an author**, unless you actually want writes; separating the two

jobs keeps the diff auditable.

- **Use structured outputs** when a later step needs to branch on the result rather than

scraping prose.

FAQ

**Where does the action run?** On your own GitHub runner. Only the Anthropic API calls (or your chosen cloud provider's) leave your infrastructure.

**Which authentication methods are supported?** Anthropic direct API via API key or workload identity federation, plus Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry.

**Does it need configuration to know when to run?** No - mode detection is automatic from the workflow context (mentions, assignments, explicit prompts).

**How do I control what Claude can do?** Through `claude_args`, passing Claude Code flags including the allowed-tools list.

**Migrating from v0.x?** There is a migration guide for step-by-step upgrade; most existing setups are compatible.

title: SpecKit

summary: Spec-driven development workflow that makes AI coding agents write a spec and a plan before they write code.

frontmatter.title: SpecKit
frontmatter.description: Spec-driven development workflow that makes AI coding agents write a spec and a plan before they write code.

body:
Learn more
Repository
https://github.com/github/spec-kit

Docs
https://github.com/github/spec-kit/blob/main/README.md

Overview

SpecKit is GitHub's toolkit for **spec-driven development**: instead of prompting an agent straight into code, you move through explicit stages — specification, plan, tasks, implementation — and each stage produces a file that is reviewed before the next begins.

The value is not ceremony. It is that the ambiguous decisions surface while they are still cheap to change, in a document a human can read, rather than showing up as three hundred lines of code built on a wrong assumption.

 SpecKit is agent-agnostic. It installs slash commands into whichever assistant you use — Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, and others — and the artifacts it produces are plain Markdown in your repository. 

**Use it when** the work spans multiple files, has real design decisions, or will be picked up later by someone (or something) without your context. **Skip it** for a typo fix.

Installation

SpecKit is distributed as `specify-cli` and run through `uv`, so there is nothing global to install and remove later.

<CodeGroup>

bash
`uvx --from git+https://github.com/github/spec-kit.git specify init my-project`

bash
`uvx --from git+https://github.com/github/spec-kit.git specify init --here`

</CodeGroup>

The first form scaffolds a new project directory; the second initializes the repository you are already in. During init you choose which AI assistant to target, and SpecKit writes the matching command definitions.

Check the result:

bash
`specify check`

Initialization creates a `.specify/` directory holding templates, scripts, and your project constitution, plus the assistant-specific command files.

Configuration

The two things worth configuring are the constitution and the templates.

**`.specify/memory/constitution.md`** holds the principles every feature is checked against — architecture rules, technology choices, quality gates. This is the highest-leverage file in the toolkit: the planning stage validates each design against it, so a rule written here is enforced on work you are not watching.

markdown
`### I. Static First (NON-NEGOTIABLE) No server-side runtime and no database. Any feature needing a server MUST be redesigned as a build-time solution, or rejected.`

Write principles as testable constraints. "Use good architecture" cannot be checked; "no new runtime dependency without written approval" can.

**`.specify/templates/`** holds the shape of each generated artifact — spec, plan, tasks, checklist. Edit these when your team needs a section that the defaults do not produce, such as a security review or a rollout plan.

Examples

A typical feature runs through the commands in order:

text
`/speckit.constitution # once per project — establish the rules /speckit.specify # what and why, no implementation detail /speckit.clarify # resolve ambiguities before planning /speckit.plan # tech stack, architecture, file structure /speckit.tasks # dependency-ordered, actionable task list /speckit.implement # execute the tasks`

**Specify** — describe the outcome, not the code:

text
`/speckit.specify Users can save an article to a reading list and see it on a /saved page. Saved state survives a page reload and is per-account.`

**Analyze** — before implementing, cross-check the artifacts against each other:

text
`/speckit.analyze`

This reports contradictions between spec, plan, and tasks — a requirement with no task, a task with no requirement, a plan that quietly violates the constitution.

Best Practices

- **Write the constitution first and keep it short.** Five enforceable principles beat twenty

aspirational ones.

- **Review the spec before planning.** Correcting a sentence costs seconds; correcting the

code built from it costs an afternoon.

- **Run `/speckit.clarify` on anything non-trivial.** Answering five targeted questions is

faster than reading a plan built on guesses.

- **Commit `.specify/` and `specs/`.** The artifacts are project documentation, not scratch

files — they explain to future readers why the code is shaped the way it is.

- **One feature per spec directory.** Bundling unrelated changes defeats the review step.
- **Let the plan be rejected.** If `/speckit.analyze` flags a constitution violation, fix the

design or amend the constitution deliberately — do not quietly proceed.

FAQ

**Does it only work with GitHub Copilot?** No. Despite living under the GitHub organization, SpecKit supports several assistants and asks which one you use at init time.

**Do I have to run every command?** The spec → plan → tasks → implement path is the core. `clarify`, `analyze`, and `checklist` are optional quality gates; use them on work where being wrong is expensive.

**Is this just documentation overhead?** For a one-line fix, yes — skip it. The cost is fixed and the benefit scales with how much code an agent writes unattended, so it pays off on exactly the work where review matters most.

**Can I change the workflow?** Yes. The templates in `.specify/templates/` and the command definitions are files in your repository. Edit them.

**What if I already started the feature?** Run `specify init --here` in the existing repository and write the spec for the remaining work. There is no requirement to start from an empty directory.

body:
Learn more
Repository
https://github.com/obra/superpowers

Docs
https://github.com/obra/superpowers/blob/main/README.md

Overview

Superpowers is a full development **methodology** packaged as composable skills plus the initial instructions that make an agent actually use them. Rather than reaching for code, the agent first asks what you are really trying to do, teases a spec out of the conversation, shows it to you in digestible chunks, and waits for sign-off before touching anything.

After the design is approved it produces an implementation plan written to be followed by "an enthusiastic junior engineer with poor taste, no judgement, no project context, and an aversion to testing" - emphasizing red/green TDD, YAGNI and DRY - and then runs a subagent-driven development process where agents work each task and inspect and review the work as they go. The README reports agents working autonomously for a couple of hours at a time without deviating from the agreed plan.

Because the skills trigger automatically, there is nothing to remember to invoke.

Installation

Superpowers is available through Anthropic's official Claude plugin marketplace:

bash
`/plugin install superpowers@claude-plugins-official`

The project also runs its own marketplace, and installation is **per harness** - if you use more than one coding agent, install it separately for each. The README documents setup paths for Claude Code, Antigravity, Codex App, Codex CLI, Cursor, Devin CLI, Factory Droid, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot CLI, Grok Build CLI, Kimi Code, OpenCode, Pi, Qwen Code and Hermes Agent.

Configuration

There is no configuration to speak of - the value is the composable skill set rather than a settings file. What matters is the order the methodology runs in: elicitation, spec review, plan approval, then subagent-driven execution.

If your harness supports plugins natively, the plugin bundles the skills and the trigger instructions together so the agent follows the sequence without configuration.

Examples

The practical pattern is "ask, review, approve":

- **Kick off elicitation** - describe the feature in conversation rather than writing a spec

by hand. The agent asks clarifying questions instead of assuming.

- **Review the spec in chunks** - short enough to actually read, so the review is real rather

than a rubber stamp.

- **Approve the plan** - the plan is written for a junior engineer without context, which is

how you find the steps you forgot to specify.

- **Let it execute** - subagents work the tasks with review between them.

Best Practices

- **Do not skip the design conversation.** The elicitation step is where the expensive

misunderstandings get caught.

- **Read the spec chunks properly.** Approving a spec you skimmed is the failure mode; the

chunking exists so you can actually read it.

- **Use it for multi-file work.** For a one-line fix the methodology is pure overhead.
- **Review the plan for the gaps you omitted.** The plan is deliberately written for someone

with no context, so anything you did not state shows up as a step someone cannot execute.

- **Install per harness.** Each agent has its own installation; expect to do it more than once.

FAQ

**Is this just prompt engineering?** It is a packaged method expressed as skills, so the prompts are the mechanism - but the value is the sequence and the automatic triggering, not the individual instructions.

**Does it only work with Claude Code?** No. The README documents installation for a wide range of harnesses, including Codex CLI, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI and Copilot.

**Do I have to invoke the skills manually?** No - the README is explicit that because the skills trigger automatically, you do not need to do anything special beyond having the skills installed.

**What happens when something goes wrong?** The README has a "When Something Goes Wrong" section covering recovering when an agent deviates; the loop is designed to pause for human approval at design boundaries rather than charging ahead.

**Is commercial support available?** Yes - the project points enterprise users to a support contact for commercial services.

body:
Learn more
Repository
https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/fetch

Package
mcp-server-fetch

Docs
https://pypi.org/project/mcp-server-fetch/

The fetch server gives an agent one capability: retrieve a web page and return it as markdown rather than raw HTML, which is far cheaper for a model to read. It is one of the reference servers maintained with the protocol.

 The server's own README carries an explicit caution: it can reach local and internal IP addresses and may represent a security risk. Keep that in mind before connecting it anywhere sensitive - and read the prompt-injection note before using it for research. 

Installation

Through `uvx` with no separate install step:

bash
`uvx mcp-server-fetch`

Or via pip:

bash
`pip install mcp-server-fetch python -m mcp_server_fetch`

Installing Node.js optionally enables a different HTML simplifier the server considers more robust.

Configuration

No configuration is required - the server takes no arguments and no credentials. The configuration that matters is the client's, and it is a security decision: this server can reach any URL the machine can reach, including internal ones.

Per the README it requires MCP Python SDK 1.x (`mcp>=1.29.0,<2`); a port to SDK 2.0 is in progress.

Usage

One tool, `fetch`, with four arguments:

ArgumentTypeDefaultPurpose
`url`stringrequiredThe URL to fetch
`max_length`integer5000Maximum characters returned
`start_index`integer0Where to start extracting
`raw`booleanfalseReturn content without markdown conversion

`start_index` is the feature that makes it usable: the response is truncated, so a model can request the next chunk and keep reading until it finds what it needs, rather than losing the tail of a long page.

The server also registers a `fetch` **prompt** taking a `url` argument.

Examples

**Read a documentation page**

text
`What does the official docs say about configuring authentication for this API?`

**Read past the truncation**

text
`Fetch the changelog and keep reading further down - I want the entries from the last six months.`

**Compare two pages**

text
`Compare the pricing sections of these two pages and tell me what changed.`

**A real risk to plan for**

Because the agent reads arbitrary web pages into its context, treat every fetched page as untrusted input - it is a channel through which instructions can arrive. OWASP ranks prompt injection as the top LLM risk and notes retrieved content is one such channel. The practical mitigation is not better filtering but permissions: require approval for anything outward-facing the agent might do after reading an attacker-controlled page.

body:
Learn more
Repository
https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/filesystem

Package
@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem

Docs
https://modelcontextprotocol.io

The filesystem server is one of the reference MCP servers maintained alongside the protocol itself. It gives a model file operations — read, write, list, search, move — scoped to directories you name explicitly. Everything outside those roots is invisible to it.

It is the server most people install first, because it is small enough to read end to end and it makes the access model concrete: the allowed directories are arguments, not settings buried somewhere.

 The directories you pass on the command line are the entire security boundary. A server started with your home directory as its root can read every file in it. Scope it to the project you are working on. 

Installation

The server runs through `npx`, so there is nothing to install ahead of time — the client launches it on demand. You need Node.js 18 or newer.

For Claude Code:

bash
`claude mcp add filesystem -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem ~/projects/my-app`

For any client that uses the standard JSON config format, add an entry under `mcpServers`:

json
`{ "mcpServers": { "filesystem": { "command": "npx", "args": [ "-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/Users/you/projects/my-app" ] } } }`

Restart the client after editing its config. In Claude Code, confirm the server came up with:

bash
`claude mcp list`

Configuration

Every argument after the package name is an allowed root directory. There is no wildcard and no "allow everything" flag — that is deliberate.

**Multiple roots** — pass one path per directory:

json
`{ "mcpServers": { "filesystem": { "command": "npx", "args": [ "-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/Users/you/projects/api", "/Users/you/projects/web" ] } } }`

**Windows paths** need escaped backslashes in JSON, or forward slashes:

json
`"args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "C:/Users/you/projects/my-app"]`

**Read-only usage** is not a server flag. If you want the model to read but never write, do not rely on configuration — point it at a copy, or use your client's per-tool permission settings to deny the write tools.

Paths are resolved before access checks, so symlinks pointing outside an allowed root are rejected rather than followed.

Usage

Once connected, the server advertises its tools and the model calls them when a request needs them. You do not invoke tools by name; you describe the task.

Typical requests that route through this server:

- "Read `src/config.ts` and tell me which environment variables it expects."
- "Search this project for files that still import the old logger."
- "Write the migration notes to `docs/migration.md`."

The tools it exposes cover reading files, writing and editing files, creating directories, listing directory contents, moving files, searching by pattern, and reading file metadata.

Two things worth knowing about behaviour:

- Directory listings distinguish files from directories, so the model can walk a tree without

guessing.

- Search matches paths against a glob pattern rather than scanning file contents — pair it

with a read when you need to match on what is inside a file.

Examples

**Scope the server to one repository**

bash
`claude mcp add fs-api -- npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem ~/code/api`

Naming the server after the project (`fs-api`) makes it obvious which root is mounted when you have several configured.

**Separate read and write roots**

json
`{ "mcpServers": { "filesystem": { "command": "npx", "args": [ "-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/Users/you/projects/app/src", "/Users/you/projects/app/docs" ] } } }`

Mounting `src` and `docs` rather than the project root keeps `.env`, `.git`, and `node_modules` out of reach without any extra configuration.

**Verify the boundary before trusting it**

Ask the model to read a file you know is outside the allowed roots. The call should fail with an access error. Testing the negative case takes ten seconds and tells you more than reading the config does.

body:
Learn more
Repository
https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/git

Package
mcp-server-git

Docs
https://pypi.org/project/mcp-server-git/

The git server lets an agent read, search and change a Git repository through MCP tools - status, diffs, logs, commits, branches. It is one of the reference servers maintained alongside the protocol itself.

 The reference servers repository is explicit that these are **educational reference implementations**, not production-ready solutions - developers should evaluate their own security requirements for their threat model. Treat this one the same way you would any third-party code you are about to run with repository write access. 

It is also worth pairing with the filesystem server rather than choosing between them: git handles history and diffs, filesystem handles the working tree.

Installation

The server runs through `uvx` with no separate install step:

bash
`uvx mcp-server-git --repository /path/to/repo`

Or via pip:

bash
`pip install mcp-server-git python -m mcp_server_git --repository /path/to/repo`

You need Python available. Per the README the server requires MCP Python SDK 1.x (`mcp>=1.29.0,<2`); SDK 2.0 renamed APIs this server uses and a port is in progress.

Configuration

The repository path is passed as a command-line argument, either with `--repository` or as a positional path. This server's tool contract differs from the filesystem server: **every tool takes a `repo_path` argument**, so the model passes the repository on each call rather than the server being bound to one path at launch.

Usage

Once connected, the agent gets these tools. Each takes `repo_path` (and any other listed argument):

- **Read:** `git_status`, `git_diff_unstaged`, `git_diff_staged`, `git_diff`, `git_log`
- **Write:** `git_commit`, `git_add`, `git_reset`, `git_create_branch`, `git_checkout`,

`git_show`

A few shapes worth knowing:

- Diffs accept an optional `context_lines` (default 3) so the agent can widen the window when

it needs more surrounding context.

- `git_log` takes `max_count` (default 10) plus optional `start_timestamp` and

`end_timestamp` filters, which accept ISO 8601 (`2024-01-15T14:30:25`), relative (`2 weeks ago`, `yesterday`) or absolute (`2024-01-15`, `Jan 15 2024`) dates.

- `git_create_branch` takes `branch_name` and an optional `base_branch` (defaults to the

current branch).

- `git_reset` unstages all staged changes.

You do not invoke these by name - you describe the task and the model chooses.

Examples

**Ask about the working tree**

text
`What has changed but not been committed in this repo, and does anything look accidental?`

**Trace when a line appeared**

text
`When was the retry logic in api.py first added? Use the git history.`

**Branch and commit deliberately**

text
`Create a branch called fix/timeouts, stage only the timeout files, and commit them.`

**Time-bounded history**

text
`What was merged in the last two weeks, and what do the commit messages say changed?`

Because the write tools are real Git operations, scope the repository path to the project you are working on and let the host require approval for commits and branch operations.

body:
Learn more
Repository
https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/memory

Package
@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory

Docs
https://modelcontextprotocol.io

The memory server gives an agent a persistent, local knowledge graph so it can remember things about you across separate chats. It is a reference server, and its data model is the whole design.

Three concepts carry it:

- **Entities** - nodes with a unique `name`, an `entityType` (person, organization, event),

and a list of observations.

- **Relations** - directed connections between entities, always stored in **active voice**

(`works_at`, not `works_at_in`), describing how entities relate.

- **Observations** - atomic strings attached to one entity, one fact each, added or removed

independently.

 The "atomic observation" rule is what makes this usable. Storing "speaks fluent Spanish, graduated in 2019, prefers morning meetings" as three observations means you can remove one fact without destroying the other two. A single blob observation cannot be edited surgically. 

Installation

Through `npx` with no separate install step:

bash
`npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-memory`

The server writes to a local JSONL file, so no database is needed. The Docker variant mounts a volume at `/app/dist` to persist it.

Configuration

Configuration is minimal - the server accepts a path for its memory file if you want it somewhere other than the default. Everything else is behaviour:

- The graph is **local and plain-text**. Review it, and delete lines from the file directly

if you disagree with what it recorded.

- Relations must be active voice and must connect existing entities, so the graph cannot

accumulate dangling edges.

Usage

The server exposes tools for each operation:

- **Create:** `create_entities`, `create_relations`
- **Add:** `add_observations`
- **Delete:** `delete_entities` (cascading to its relations), `delete_observations`,

`delete_relations`

Behaviour worth knowing, per the README:

- `create_entities` **ignores** entities whose names already exist rather than overwriting.
- `create_relations` skips duplicates, and **fails** if either endpoint does not exist.
- `delete_entities` cascades to related relations and **does not error** on a missing name -

it reports which names were not found.

- `delete_observations` and `delete_relations` similarly report rather than error.

You do not call these by name. You talk to the model, and it decides what to remember.

Examples

**"Remember that I prefer pnpm"**

text
`Remember that I use pnpm, not npm, and that my Node version is pinned in .nvmrc.`

**"What do you know about my project conventions?"**

text
`What do you remember about how I like this codebase structured?`

**Correct a stored fact**

text
`Actually I've moved to Bun now - update that.`

**Inspect and prune**

The memory file is plain text, so open it, read what the agent decided was worth keeping, and delete lines you disagree with. That review step is the point - an unexamined memory is a record of what the agent inferred, not what you said.

body:
Learn more
Repository
https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/sequentialthinking

Package
@modelcontextprotocol/server-sequential-thinking

Docs
https://modelcontextprotocol.io

The sequential thinking server exposes a single tool, `sequential_thinking`, that structures a problem as an ordered sequence of thoughts the model can revise and branch as its understanding deepens. It is one of the reference servers maintained with the protocol.

The point is not to make the model think more - it is to make the thinking **inspectable and correctable**. Each step is a separate record, so a wrong turn can be explicitly revised rather than silently absorbed into the next step.

Installation

Through `npx` with no separate install step:

bash
`npx -y @modelcontextprotocol/server-sequential-thinking`

Configuration

No configuration is required; the server takes no arguments. The behaviour is in the tool arguments, which the model fills in:

ArgumentTypePurpose
`thought`stringThe current thinking step
`thoughtNumber`integerWhich step this is
`totalThoughts`integerEstimated number of steps
`nextThoughtNeeded`booleanWhether to continue
`isRevision`booleanWhether this revisits an earlier step
`revisesThought`integerWhich step is being reconsidered
`branchFromThought`integerWhere this branch starts
`branchId`stringBranch identifier

`totalThoughts` is an estimate the model adjusts as it goes - that is what lets the sequence grow when the problem turns out to be bigger than expected.

Usage

The tool is designed for: breaking complex problems into steps; planning and design with room for revision; analysis that may need course correction; problems whose full scope is not clear at the start; and tasks where irrelevant information must be filtered out.

Per the README, you normally do not call it by hand - you connect the server to an MCP-aware host and ask the model to work through a problem step by step. The host decides when to call it, possibly several times.

To confirm it is running, look for repeated `sequential_thinking` calls with `thought`, `thoughtNumber`, `totalThoughts` and `nextThoughtNeeded` in your host's tool activity or an inspector; revision and branching add `isRevision`, `revisesThought`, `branchFromThought` or `branchId`.

Examples

**Migration with a stated constraint**

text
`Plan a database migration from PostgreSQL 14 to 16, list the risks, and revise the plan if downtime would exceed 5 minutes.`

**Environment-specific bug**

text
`Debug why this deployment only fails in production, and show your reasoning step by step.`

**Branching comparison**

text
`Compare three architecture options for a file sync engine, and branch if one of your assumptions turns out to be wrong.`

A fair caveat: this server adds latency and tokens because every step is a recorded tool call. It earns its cost on open-ended analysis; on a task with a known shape, the extra turns are overhead.

frontmatter.title: Time MCP Server
frontmatter.description: Reference MCP server giving an agent the current time and timezone conversion using IANA timezone names.

body:
Learn more
Repository
https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/servers/tree/main/src/time

Package
mcp-server-time

Docs
https://pypi.org/project/mcp-server-time/

The time server is the smallest reference server in the collection: two tools, current time and timezone conversion. It exists because a model has no clock - asking it what time it is returns a plausible guess, and asking it to convert between timezones without a reference is worse.

It uses **IANA timezone names** (`America/New_York`, `Europe/London`) and supports automatic system timezone detection.

 This is a good first server after the filesystem one precisely because it is small enough to read end to end, and it demonstrates the whole MCP tool contract without any credential or network handling. 

Installation

Through `uvx` with no separate install step:

bash
`uvx mcp-server-time`

Or via pip:

bash
`pip install mcp-server-time python -m mcp_server_time`

The Docker variant takes a `LOCAL_TIMEZONE` environment variable to set the default zone.

Configuration

No credentials and no arguments for the basic setup. The one configuration decision that matters is `LOCAL_TIMEZONE`, which sets the system default used when no timezone is given.

Per the README the server requires MCP Python SDK 1.x (`mcp>=1.29.0,<2`); a port to SDK 2.0 is in progress.

Usage

Two tools, both requiring IANA timezone names:

- **`get_current_time`** - current time in a specific timezone, or the system timezone.

Requires `timezone` (string).

- **`convert_time`** - convert between timezones. Requires `source_timezone`, `time` (24-hour

`HH:MM`) and `target_timezone`.

Ask for the thing you want; the model fills in the arguments.

Examples

**"What time is it in Tokyo?"**

text
`What time is it in Tokyo right now?`

**Scheduling across zones**

text
`It's 9am in London - what time should I schedule the call for someone in San Francisco?`

**Daylight-saving correctness**

text
`The release is at 15:00 UTC. Convert that to Berlin and confirm the offset.`

Because a wrong timezone assumption silently produces a wrong answer rather than an error, it is worth confirming the zone name in the agent's reply when the answer will be acted on.

body:
This page is maintained by hand and is never edited by automation. Offers change without notice — always confirm the current terms on the provider's own page before you plan around them. 

Anthropic runs a startup program that provides API credits alongside technical support for teams building products on Claude. Credits are granted through an application, and access is also distributed through accelerators and venture partners that run their own perks programs.

What you get

Credit amounts are not published as a fixed number — they depend on the program you come through and the stage of the company. Beyond credits, the program is oriented around onboarding help: guidance on model selection, prompt and evaluation practices, and a path to raise rate limits as usage grows.

Who is eligible

Eligibility is judged case by case, but the shape is consistent:

- An early-stage company, typically pre-Series B
- A product that actually calls the Claude API — not an idea in a deck
- An application that passes review

If your accelerator, incubator, or lead investor has an Anthropic partnership, applying through them is usually faster than applying cold.

How to apply

- Read the current terms on the Anthropic for Startups page.
- Check whether your accelerator or investor already offers Anthropic credits — partner

routes are generally quicker and sometimes more generous.

- Submit the application with a concrete description of what you are building and where

Claude fits.

- If approved, credits are applied to your organization in the

Claude Console.

Before you rely on it

- **Credits expire.** Terms vary by program; confirm the window when you are approved and

plan usage against it.

- **Have a paid path ready.** Build cost tracking from the start (`usage` is on every API

response) so the transition off credits is a known number, not a surprise.

- **Approval is not instant.** Do not schedule a launch that depends on credits arriving by

a particular date.

**Related:** Set up your Claude API key covers creating the account and key the credits are applied to.

summary: How to write success criteria that survive reality, and how to pick a scoring method that will not lie to you.

frontmatter.title: Evaluating AI Output
frontmatter.description: How to write success criteria that survive reality, and how to pick a scoring method that will not lie to you.

body:
What you will be able to do
- Write success criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable, and relevant to the actual task.
- Choose between deterministic checks, fuzzy metrics, model-as-judge, and human review.
- Build a small eval harness that compares two candidates and reports per-case detail.
- Recognise the eval anti-patterns that produce confident, meaningless scores.

Testing an AI system feels like testing software, and the resemblance is exactly where projects go wrong. A function that takes an int and returns an int has a contract. A model that writes a support reply has a distribution over plausible replies, and "does it work" does not have a boolean answer.

That does not make evaluation impossible. It makes it a different discipline: you are not asserting truth, you are *measuring a rate* against criteria you chose deliberately.

What this module covers

The first session is about writing the criteria before you write the test. Most eval projects fail here and spend the rest of their life chasing a number that measures the wrong thing. Anthropic's guidance is blunt about this: define success criteria and ways to test against them *before* writing the first prompt.

The second session works through the scoring methods in order of how much you should trust them — exact and structural checks, then fuzzy overlap metrics, then model-as-judge, then human review — with a runnable harness that shows what each one actually detects.

 The single most useful thing in this module is a failure mode, not a technique. Overlap metrics like token F1 reward length: a candidate can improve its score by padding an answer with restatement. Module 3's grounding example shows the same weakness in a different place — a bag-of-words check passes a claim where "30 days" silently became "14 days". Any single metric can be gamed, which is why serious evals are a small set of metrics plus at least one hard gate. 

What you should be able to do afterwards

- Take a vague requirement and turn it into a criterion you could actually fail.
- Write ~20 eval cases in under an hour for a real feature.
- Justify your scoring method, or say plainly that you are using the easiest available

one because the task is open-ended.

Official resources
- Evaluation best practices
- Define success criteria and build evaluations

body:
What you will be able to do
- Explain generative AI as next-token prediction, and why that framing predicts both its strengths and its failure modes.
- Describe how training and inference differ, and what a model does and does not retain from your prompts.
- Identify hallucination triggers and design prompts and workflows that make them rarer and easier to catch.
- Choose and read an evaluation method that fits a task, rather than picking a metric by habit.
- Budget a context window deliberately instead of discovering the limit through a failed request.

Modules
4·8 sessions·185 min

- 01What Is Generative AI?

What actually happens when you send a prompt, and the three ideas — training, inference, model — that people blur together.
- 01Next-Token Prediction: The Actual Mechanism
Build next-token prediction from word counts alone, then see how the same idea scales to modern language models.

25′
- 02Training, Inference, and the Model Artifact
The three ideas public discussion blurs — training, inference, and the weights on disk — and what each one can and cannot change.

20′

- 02LLM Fundamentals

Tokens, context windows, logits, sampling and temperature — the machinery that decides what your model can see and how confidently it speaks.
- 01Tokens and the Context Window
How text becomes tokens, why the count differs from words or characters, and how to budget a context window before you hit the limit.

25′
- 02Inference and Sampling
What happens between 'the prompt arrived' and 'the sentence exists' — logits, softmax, sampling, temperature, top-k and top-p.

25′

- 03Model Limitations and Hallucinations

Where confident false statements come from, what makes them worse, and the mitigation techniques that genuinely help.
- 01Why Models Confidently Fabricate
Where a fabricated citation actually comes from, which errors are most dangerous, and the prompt conditions that raise hallucination rates.

25′
- 02Mitigating Hallucinations
The mitigation toolkit — grounding, permission to refuse, quote-first extraction, citations, verification — and the honest limits of each.

25′

- 04Evaluating AI Output

How to write success criteria that survive reality, and how to pick a scoring method that will not lie to you.
- 01Define Success Criteria Before You Write the Test
Turn a vague requirement into a criterion you could actually fail, and build the eval dataset that tests it.

20′
- 02Choosing a Scoring Method
Exact checks, fuzzy metrics, model-as-judge and human review — what each detects, and which metric will quietly lie to you.

20′

Most people meet generative AI as a chat box and leave it there. That is enough to be impressed and not enough to use it. This course goes one level down: it builds the mechanism first, then spends as much time on where that mechanism breaks as on what it can do.

The order matters. If you learn "how to prompt" before you know that a language model is a next-token predictor trained to continue text, every prompting trick you learn becomes a superstition. Once the mechanism is clear, prompt structure stops being folklore and starts being context engineering.

Who this is for

You can write code, or you can at least read it, and you have used a chat assistant. You do not need linear algebra, and you will not be asked to train anything. Roughly three hours of reading and running short scripts.

You are *not* expected to arrive with opinions about which AI company is best. Model names change several times a year; the mechanism described here does not.

How the course is built

Four modules, two sessions each. Module 1 answers *what is actually happening when I press send*. Module 2 covers the machinery — tokens, context, inference, sampling. Module 3 is the uncomfortable one: hallucinations, and the design choices that cause them. Module 4 turns all of it into a repeatable practice you can run on your own work.

 The examples in this course are real programs you can run, not pseudocode. Every output quoted in the prose was produced by executing the snippet. Where a claim depends on a current product detail — a model name, a parameter, an API shape — the source is linked in `official_resources` rather than asserted from memory. 

The modules

<Accordion title="Module 1 — What is generative AI?"> Two sessions. The first dismantles the magic without being condescending about it, and shows that a genuinely small program can produce uncannily fluent text from pure statistics. The second separates three ideas that get used interchangeably and should not be: training, inference, and a model as a fixed artifact. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Module 2 — LLM fundamentals"> Two sessions on the machinery. Tokens and the context window, including the arithmetic that decides whether your request fits. Then inference: logits, softmax, sampling, temperature, and why "ask it again" is sometimes a legitimate technique and sometimes a way to launder a wrong answer. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Module 3 — Limitations and hallucinations"> Two sessions on failure. Where false confident statements actually come from, and what makes them worse. Then the mitigation toolkit: grounding, permission to refuse, quoting before answering, and verification — each with the honest note about what it does not fix. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Module 4 — Evaluating AI output"> Two sessions on judgement. How to write success criteria that survive contact with reality, and how to pick a scoring method — deterministic checks, fuzzy metrics, model- as-judge, and human review — including which metric will lie to you. </Accordion>

A working habit from module 1

Before you build anything on a model, you should be able to answer these four questions about your own use case:

- What is the exact input, and what is an acceptable output?
- What would a correct answer look like if you wrote it yourself?
- Which part of the answer could be wrong without anyone noticing immediately?
- How would you find out that it was wrong?

If you cannot answer 3 and 4, you are not ready to put it in front of users. Module 4 turns questions 2 and 4 into an actual test suite. Everything before that exists so the answers to 1 and 3 are honest.

Where to go next

This course is deliberately vendor-neutral and mechanism-first. After Module 2 you should be able to read any provider's API reference and understand what every parameter does, whichever one you use. Provider-specific setup lives elsewhere on AI Hub.

body:
What you will be able to do
- Explain tokens, tokenizers, and why token counts differ from word or character counts.
- Budget a context window deliberately, accounting for system prompts, history, tool schemas and output.
- Describe what happens at inference time: logits, softmax, sampling, temperature, top-k and top-p.
- Judge when stochastic sampling is the right choice and when it is a reliability bug.

This module is the plumbing. Once you have it, provider API references stop being a wall of unfamiliar parameters and become a short list of decisions you can make deliberately.

Two sessions. The first covers what the model can see: tokens, tokenizers, and the context window as a single shared budget that your prompt, your history, your tool definitions and the model's own output all draw from. The second covers how it decides what to say next: logits, sampling, and the parameters that reshape that decision.

Why this is not the boring part

Two misunderstandings cause a lot of wasted work.

The first is thinking the context window is about how much you can paste in. It is about that, but it is more precisely a *budget with line items*, and the line items are surprising: tool definitions and the model's output count too. Teams are routinely surprised by a request failing on output length after carefully trimming input.

The second is treating sampling parameters as quality dials. They are not. They change the *shape of the distribution* the model samples from — how much probability mass survives outside the leading candidate — and whether that helps depends entirely on your task. The same setting that produces useful variation in a brainstorm is a defect in a JSON parser.

 A practical note that will matter more than the theory: on Claude 4.7 and later models, `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k` are not supported, and setting them to a non-default value returns a 400 error. Anthropic's guidance is to omit them and shape behaviour with the prompt instead. The sampling machinery is still the right mental model — you are choosing whether to treat the model as deterministic or as stochastic — but check the provider's current migration notes before you send sampling parameters. See the `official_resources` on this page. 

What you should be able to do afterwards

- Estimate whether a request will fit in a context window before sending it, and say

which line items are consuming the budget.

- Explain to a non-engineer why "temperature 0.7" is not a quality setting.
- Read the `usage` block on any API response and tell what it charged you for.

- Using the Messages API

body:
What you will be able to do
- Explain hallucination as a consequence of next-token prediction rather than a random defect.
- Identify prompt and system-design conditions that measurably increase hallucination rates.
- Apply grounding, explicit permission to refuse, quote-first extraction, and verification.
- Be honest about which mitigations reduce errors and which only change their appearance.

Every module so far has been about what the mechanism can do. This one is about where that mechanism lies to you, and it is the module most worth the time.

Hallucination gets discussed as though it were a bug in the same sense as a memory leak. It is not. It is the predictable behaviour of a system optimised to produce plausible continuations, asked a question it cannot answer from what it has. Understanding that changes what you do about it.

What this module covers

The first session is diagnostic. It traces where a fabricated citation actually comes from, and shows with runnable code that the most dangerous errors are the small ones — a changed number, an invented product name — not the wild fabrications people expect. It also covers the structural causes: unanswerable questions, context that does not contain the answer, and prompts that demand a format with no "I don't know" option.

The second session is the mitigation toolkit, drawn from Anthropic's published guidance. Grounding answers in supplied documents, giving explicit permission to say "I don't know", asking for verbatim quotes before analysis, requiring citations, and verification passes.

 The uncomfortable part, stated up front: none of these techniques eliminates hallucination. Anthropic's own documentation says so. They reduce the rate and, just as importantly, change *what the failure looks like* — a model that cites its source gives you something to check, while a confident unsourced paragraph gives you nothing. Design for the second case explicitly, because it is the one that reaches a user. 

The honest hierarchy of mitigations

From most to least effective, roughly:

- **Do not ask the question.** If a model is not the right tool for a task, no prompt

makes it reliable.

- **Give it the answer's source.** Most fact-grounded failures are context failures.
- **Give it permission to fail.** Models that may decline decline much more often than

models that are forbidden from declining.

- **Force the reasoning out.** Asking for the intermediate extract makes the source

contact auditable.

- **Verify independently.** Second pass, different method, or human review.

Only the fifth is a guarantee. Everything above it is a reduction in probability.

What you should be able to do afterwards

- Look at a prompt someone wrote and name the specific conditions that make

hallucination more likely.

- Build a factual-answer prompt that returns citations you can mechanically check.
- Explain to a stakeholder why "it hallucinates less" is not the same as "it is correct".

Official resources

- Citations

body:
What you will be able to do
- Explain generative AI as next-token prediction and predict its failure modes from that framing.
- Run a small model that produces fluent text from counts alone, with no neural network.
- Distinguish training, inference, and the artifact, and say what each one does and does not change.

The point of this module is to replace a vibe with a mechanism. Not to make you an expert — to make you suspicious of explanations that do not survive contact with one.

The single most useful idea in applied AI is this: **a language model is a conditional probability distribution over its next token, and everything else is engineering wrapped around that fact.** Grounding, prompt structure, retrieval, tool use, evaluation — all of it exists to shape what the distribution puts its mass on.

What this module covers

Two sessions, about 45 minutes in total.

The first session builds the idea from a program with no neural network in it, then explains how the same idea scales to models with hundreds of billions of parameters. It also addresses the reasonable objection that counting words cannot produce coherent prose, because that objection is correct about a bigram model and the resolution is interesting.

The second session draws three lines that public discussion constantly blurs: the difference between *training* and *inference*, the difference between *the model* and *the weights on your disk*, and the difference between *what the model knows* and *what you gave it this conversation*. Getting these straight prevents a whole category of "the AI learned something wrong yesterday" confusion.

What you should be able to do afterwards

- Look at any AI feature and say which part is the model and which part is scaffolding.
- Explain why a model can be fluent and still confidently wrong.
- Tell a teammate why they do not need to "retrain" something to change a system prompt,

and when they genuinely do need fine-tuning.

A note on scope

This module does not cover embeddings, fine-tuning, or retrieval. Those are real and useful, but they are downstream of the mechanism established here, and presenting them early is what produces the cargo-cult prompting culture this course is trying to fix.

title: Context and Evidence
description: Decide what the model can see: what enters context, what stays on disk, and what it will never know.
summary: Decide what the model can see: what enters context, what stays on disk, and what it will never know.

frontmatter.title: Context and Evidence
frontmatter.description: Decide what the model can see: what enters context, what stays on disk, and what it will never know.

body:
What you will be able to do
- Enumerate every channel information can reach the model through, and the ones it cannot.
- Choose between system prompt, user turn, file on disk, and retrieval for a given fact.
- Order long inputs deliberately instead of appending them.
- Write a grounding clause that forbids reasoning about unopened code.

The most expensive prompt defect is invisible from the prompt. The model gives a confident, plausible, wrong answer about a function that exists, and nothing in the text you sent was wrong. The defect is that the function was never in context.

This module is about the *availability* of information, which is a different axis from relevance or importance. A fact can be maximally important to the task and still not be available to the model.

The context window is a working memory, not a library

Anthropic's context window documentation makes two points that should govern how you write specifications.

First: the context window is a *working memory* — "all the text a language model can reference when generating a response, including the response itself". Everything counts, including your system prompt, every message, tool definitions, and the output the model is about to generate.

Second, and less comfortable: **more context is not automatically better**. The same page names the degradation — as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade, a phenomenon called *context rot*. This is why "just paste the whole repository" fails: it does not fail by running out of room, it fails by burying the signal.

 The counter-intuitive result from Anthropic's long-context guidance: put long documents at the *top* of the prompt and the query at the *end*, and queries at the end improved response quality by up to 30% in their testing. Material that matters most should be closest to the instruction that uses it. 

The visibility audit

Before you write a task, answer one question: for every fact the task depends on, which of these is true?

- It is in the conversation already.
- It will be in the context because a tool returns it.
- It is on disk and something will read it.
- **Nobody will provide it.**

That last category is the whole module. A specification that depends on a fourth-category fact is not a specification — it is a hope.

What you should be able to do afterwards

- Look at any agent session and name the channels information flowed through.
- Decide whether a fact belongs in the prompt, in a file, or in a retrieval step.
- Order a long-context prompt by influence rather than by convenience.
