questions.prompt: A team has spent two weeks tuning a summarisation prompt by reading outputs and adjusting wording until they look right, without keeping a fixed set of test cases. What is the strongest criticism of this process?

options.label: There is no fixed set of inputs with known-good outputs, so no change can be shown to be an improvement, and the loop optimises for what the reviewers noticed rather than for the cases that actually fail.
Prompt tuning is only valid when it uses a published benchmark, so a team-specific test set cannot justify a change.
Human review is too slow for a two-week iteration loop and should be replaced with model-as-judge scoring.
The problem is the wording being tuned rather than the structure, so the prompt should be rewritten from scratch.

questions.prompt: Which statements about choosing an evaluation method are correct?

options.label: Human review is the reliable option but is slow and expensive, which is why it is usually reserved for the cases a cheaper method cannot judge.
A model used as a judge is cheap and fast enough to score every run, but it shares the blind spots of the model family it judges, so it must be checked against human labels before it is trusted.
Checks that need no judgement at all, such as JSON validity, citation presence or a forbidden-phrase list, are the cheapest place to start because they fail loudly and cost nothing to run.
Model-as-judge removes the need for human labels, since a fluent model's score is more consistent than a human's.
A single average score over all cases is enough to decide whether a change helped.

questions.prompt: A candidate answer that restates the reference answer verbatim will score about the same token-level F1 as a concise paraphrase making the same claim.

options.label: True
False

questions.prompt: Your team wants a defensible claim about which of two support agents is better. Which plan actually produces one?
questions.scenario: A team ships a support agent that answers customer questions from a documentation set. A competitor's agent answers the same questions, and a reviewer comparing them says the competitor 'feels better' but cannot name a case where it is better. The team's own answers look fine in the demos. The team now wants a defensible claim about which agent is better. Which plan actually produces one?

options.label: Build a fixed set of real support questions, including the ones the current agent gets wrong, with reference answers from the documentation; score both agents on the same rubric per case, slice the results by question type, and have humans spot-check agreement between the rubric scores and their own judgement.
Show twenty users both agents side by side on their own questions and take a majority preference as the verdict.
Compare response latency and cost per query, and report whichever agent wins on those metrics as the better agent.
Reuse the questions the competitor publishes in its own marketing, so the comparison is on their chosen ground.

questions.prompt: Match each evaluation technique to what it is actually measuring. Each description is used once and every term has exactly one match.

options.label: Deterministic check

Held-out split
A rule applied to the output with no judgement involved: valid JSON, every claim carrying a citation, no banned phrase. Cheap, repeatable, and blind to everything it does not encode.
Scoring outputs in bulk with a model given the same rubric a human would use. Fast and scalable, valid only to the extent it agrees with human labels on your task.
People scoring cases against a written rubric, applied to the cases that decide whether a change ships. Slow and expensive, and still the reference the others are measured against.
Cases kept out of the tuning loop entirely, used once at the end to estimate performance on inputs nobody has optimised against.

Token counts are model-specific, so identical text costs different amounts of context in different models.
Token count is proportional to character count in any language, so context can be budgeted from file size.
Asking for a longer answer leaves proportionally less room for the input in the same window.

questions.prompt: A developer asks a model for the signature of a library function it has never been shown, and receives a plausible-looking call with arguments that do not match the real API. Which account of that output is correct?

options.label: The model is predicting a probable continuation token by token; a fluent call signature is exactly the shape it expects there, so plausibility is produced even where the fact is absent.

The answer came from an outdated version of the library's documentation in the training data.
Random sampling produced nonsense, so a lower temperature would have produced the correct call.

questions.prompt: Which situations reliably raise the chance of a hallucinated answer?

options.label: Asking about events, versions or releases that postdate the model's training data.
Asking for specifics when the prompt contains no source material for them.
Requiring an answer, with no option to say the information is unavailable.
Anything at all, provided the question is phrased clearly and the model is asked politely.
Short questions with short answers, because there is no room to hide an error.

The developer pastes it into an internal ticket. Checking the repository shows version 3.2 shipped six weeks before the model's training data ends, so the model has never seen it, and no PR or CVE with that number exists. Which response is the sound one?

options.label: Treat the whole answer as unverified, not just the date: a claim past the knowledge cutoff was fabricated, so the fix is to supply the real changelog or file as context and require the answer to quote from it, and to check each cited identifier against the source before the ticket ships.
Keep the technical detail and remove only the wrong release date, since the substance of the summary is probably sound.
Re-ask the same question with a newer model, which will have more recent training data.
Re-ask with temperature zero and require the model to state its confidence before accepting anything.

Allowing the model to say it does not know. A prompt or interface that permits an honest refusal removes the pressure to produce something plausible instead.
Checking whether expressed confidence tracks real accuracy on your own task. When it does not, confidence cannot be used as a decision threshold.
Fetching the relevant documents and placing them in context, which extends the model's usable knowledge past its training cutoff without retraining it.

Both are non-generative, because neither stores a copy of its training data.

options.label: One model can serve copywriting, summarisation and labelling-style tasks by prompting it differently, without retraining per task.
Its output must be judged against a rubric or a human, because there is no single correct string to match.
Two runs on the same prompt can differ, because the model samples from a learned distribution rather than replaying a stored answer.
It is guaranteed to produce on-brand copy that never needs human editing.
It must be trained on examples labelled with the exact tone of every brand it writes for.

questions.prompt: A colleague reports that a model's output proves the model 'understands' the text, because the text is grammatically coherent and factually correct. Which response is correct?

The colleague is right, because a factually correct answer could only come from a model that understands the material.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the inference loop and sampling are correct?

options.label: A forward pass produces a raw score for every token in the vocabulary, and softmax turns those scores into a distribution that sums to one.
Temperature reshapes how much probability mass survives outside the top token, and the top-ranked token can stay the same at every temperature.
No parameters change during inference; the same weights answer every request until the model is retrained.
Setting temperature to zero makes the model factual, because it removes the chance of an unlucky sample.
Sampling draws on more knowledge than greedy decoding, because it explores tokens the argmax would have discarded.

questions.scenario: A company updates its refund policy on Monday. On Tuesday an engineer edits a system prompt file and tells the leadership channel that the model has 'learned the new policy'. Leadership believes the change is permanent and cannot be reversed.

options.label: Correct the category error: editing the prompt changed inference, not the model. The weights never moved and could not have; the new policy lives in the context and takes effect immediately because the context column is free to edit per request, and it is equally free to revert.
The engineer is right that the change is permanent, and making it durable requires fine-tuning so the fact is written into the weights.

questions.scenario: A legal assistant is given the full 180,000-token case file in one prompt with the instruction at the very end: 'answer only from this file, and say so if the answer is not in it'. Users report that the assistant answers questions about cases outside the file and never abstains.

options.label: Treat it as a context-density problem: retrieve the relevant spans first, put the instruction immediately beside them rather than 180,000 tokens away, and keep the explicit abstention string so refusal stays a reachable continuation.
Upgrade to a larger model, since the failures are a capability limit — this file is legal text and the current model is not strong enough to reason over it.

Set the temperature to zero so the model stops producing plausible-sounding case names that are not in the file.

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis is sound?
questions.scenario: A support assistant answers 'how do I delete my account' with step-by-step instructions to change a password. It is fluent, correctly formatted, and grounded in real product vocabulary. A bag-of-words support score against the source passage gives it 0.86, and its token-F1 against the gold string scores above a version that answers the question properly. What is the sound diagnosis?

options.label: Both scores are reporting vocabulary, not truth. The assistant answered a different question, so run a hard policy gate first — the answer must not contain 'password' for this case — and treat its violation as a release blocker rather than averaging it into a score.
The support score of 0.86 is close enough to the correct answer's, so raise the pass threshold to 0.95 and the failure disappears.
Send both answers to a model-as-judge with a pinned rubric and take whichever scores higher.
Have a reviewer look at every answer before it ships, which removes the need to choose a metric at all.

questions.prompt: Which response is soundest?
questions.scenario: A team has shipped an AI summarisation feature. Its release criterion is 'token-F1 ≥ 0.6 on our eval set'. Reviewers notice that the winning version simply restates the reference answer verbatim below its own summary, pushing F1 from 0.098 to 0.795 while adding no new information, and a judge score with no human calibration has been sitting on the dashboard for months.

options.label: Treat this as a criterion problem: token-F1 rewards padding whenever the candidate reuses the reference's own words, so add hard must_include and must_not constraints, include the adversarial and known-past-failure cases, and calibrate any judge score against human review before it gates a release.
The metric works; the threshold was simply too low. Raise the bar to 0.9 and the padding trick stops paying.
Replace the fuzzy metric with a model-as-judge score, which is less gameable because it reads the meaning.
Replace both with human review of every output, and treat the numbers as advisory only.

questions.prompt: Which option is the better engineering choice, and why?
questions.scenario: A company evaluates two options for a factual internal assistant. Option A: a large model with a 500,000-token window, given the entire documentation set on every request. Option B: a smaller model given retrieved spans, instructed to answer only from the spans and to reply with a fixed abstention string when they do not contain the answer, with the API's citations feature enabled so each claim points at a character range. Which is the better engineering choice, and why?

options.label: Option B, because it makes the failure checkable: retrieved spans raise the density of relevant material, the fixed abstention string makes refusal reachable instead of fabricating, and API-extracted citations carry real pointers into the source rather than prose claims about prose.
Option A, because the larger window and larger model cover the whole knowledge base every time, so retrieval and citations are unnecessary complexity.
Option B, because retrieval guarantees only relevant material reaches the model, eliminating the possibility of a wrong answer.
Option A, because model capability determines accuracy, and a post-hoc verification pass can catch anything the model gets wrong.

body:
Definition
An AI application that runs an iterative loop — gathering context, deciding a next action, invoking tools, reading the results back into context, and repeating until the task is complete. The loop plus the host that supervises it.

Also known as
agentsagentAI agentagentic application

Why it exists
Real work has a dependency chain where each step's outcome determines the next step's input. An agent runs that chain without a human choosing each step, while leaving a human able to intervene and correct it.

How it works
Gather, decide, act, observe, repeat. The act and observe steps are where the host takes over from the model: the model emits a tool request, the host executes it, and the result becomes context for the next iteration. The host supplies the system prompt, tool set, permission model and context management. Claude Code is one such host, as is an API application built with the SDK.

Example
'Add pagination to the users endpoint and update the tests' is an agent task: locate the endpoint, read the test patterns, edit two files, run the suite, read failures, fix, repeat. Each result determines the next step and none of it fits in one response.

When to use it
When work is multi-step, the steps depend on each other, and an error should be visible and correctable. Not for a single well-specified operation, where a tool call or structured output is simpler and cheaper.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

An agent is an AI application that runs a loop — it gathers context, decides what to do, acts through tools, observes the results, and repeats until the task is done.

Why it exists

A single request/response exchange is enough for "summarise this". It is not enough for "find the bug, fix it, run the tests". Real work has a dependency chain: each step's outcome determines the next step's input. An agent exists to run that chain without a human choosing each step, while keeping a human able to intervene at any point.

How it works

The loop, in its standard shape:

- **Gather** — assemble the context for this turn.
- **Decide** — reason about what to do next.
- **Act** — call a tool.
- **Observe** — read the tool's result back into context.
- **Repeat**, or stop.

The `act` and `observe` steps are where the model leaves the text domain and the host takes over: the model emits a tool request, the host executes it, and the result becomes context for the next iteration.

The host supplies everything else around the loop — the system prompt, the tool set, the permission model, and the context management. In Claude Code that host is the CLI; in an API application it is your code plus the SDK.

 An agent is a loop plus a host. If someone says "Claude is an agent", ask which loop and which host — Claude the model is neither; it is the thing being driven. 

Claude Code's own docs are direct that the surface area of agent parallelism is broader than one feature: subagents for delegated side work inside a session, agent view for dispatching background sessions, agent teams for coordinated multi-session work, and dynamic workflows for jobs that outgrow any single approach.

When to use it

Use an agent when the work is multi-step, the steps depend on each other, and an error in step two should be visible and correctable rather than silently baked into a long answer. Do not use one for a single well-specified operation — a tool call or a structured output is simpler, cheaper and easier to verify.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not a model"> The model reasons and emits tokens. The agent is the surrounding system: the loop, the tools, the permissions, the context management, the stopping conditions. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not an MCP server"> A server exposes capabilities to an agent. The agent is the consumer. Adding an MCP server gives an existing agent new hands; it does not create an agent. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a sub-agent"> A sub-agent is one worker spawned by another agent, running in its own context. The agent is the loop that does the spawning — the parent. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not an automation"> A scheduled run is a trigger. The agent is the thing that runs when triggered. </Accordion>

Example

"Add pagination to the users endpoint and update the tests" is an agent task: find the endpoint, read the test patterns, edit two files, run the suite, read failures, fix, repeat. Each step's result determines the next. None of it can be answered in one shot.

Related concepts

- Sub-agent — a delegated worker with its own context
- Tool calling — the `act` step of the loop
- Context engineering — the `gather` step

body:
Definition
Software development in which an AI agent does substantial parts of the implementation - shifting the developer's effort from writing code to specifying behaviour, reviewing output, and verifying it mechanically.

Also known as
agentsAI-assisted developmentvibe codingagent-driven development

Why it exists
"An agent can implement faster than a developer can type, but it cannot decide

How it works
The loop is spec, implement, verify. SpecKit formalises this by requiring a specification, a plan and a dependency-ordered task list before code is written, with a constitution of principles each design is validated against. Anthropic notes the highest-leverage file in such a toolkit is the constitution, because a rule written there is enforced on work you are not watching. The verification half is mechanical: the agent runs the tests, reads failures, and fixes them.

Example
"Adding pagination to an endpoint: the agent locates the route, reads the existing test

When to use it
"Use agentic development when work spans multiple files, has real design decisions,

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Agentic development moves your effort from **typing code** to **specifying behaviour and verifying output** - because an agent implements faster than it can decide what correct means.

Why it exists

An agent's implementation speed exceeds a developer's typing speed. What it cannot do is decide what correct means - the requirement, the edge case, the trade-off. So the scarce activity shifts: less production, more specification and verification.

How it works

The loop has three parts, and the third is what makes it trustworthy.

**Specify.** The requirements are written down where they can be reviewed before code exists. SpecKit makes this a stage rather than a good habit: specification, plan, tasks, then implementation, each producing an artefact reviewed before the next begins. The value is not ceremony - it is that ambiguous decisions surface while they are still cheap to change.

**Implement.** The agent works the task list, spawning subagents where work is independent.

**Verify.** The agent runs the tests, reads failures, and iterates. This is the mechanical half, and it is what turns a plausible diff into a correct one.

 Anthropic's sharpest observation about the specify stage: the highest-leverage artefact is the constitution of principles, because a rule written there is enforced on work you are not watching. Write principles as testable constraints - "no new runtime dependency without written approval" can be checked; "use good architecture" cannot. 

When to use it

Use it when work spans multiple files, has real design decisions, or will be picked up later by someone without your context. Use a spec-first process when being wrong is expensive; skip it for a typo fix.

The economics are blunt: the process cost is fixed, and the benefit scales with how much code an agent writes unattended. That makes it pay off on exactly the work where review matters most, and be pure overhead on everything else.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not an agent"> An agent is the loop that does the work. Agentic development is the practice around it - how you scope, specify, review and verify. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a harness"> The harness is the runtime. Agentic development is the human process deciding what to hand it and how to check the result. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not an autonomous agent"> An autonomous agent runs unattended. Agentic development includes the attended case - a developer reviewing every diff is still doing it. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a skill"> A skill is packaged instructions encoding a procedure. Agentic development is a practice; skills are one way to encode parts of it. </Accordion>

Example

Adding pagination to an endpoint: the agent locates the route, reads existing test patterns, edits two files, runs the suite, reads failures and iterates. The developer's job is the spec of what pagination must do, and a review of the diff.

Related concepts

- Agent - the loop doing the work
- Eval - the gate that keeps it honest
- Hook - deterministic checks the harness runs for you

body:
Definition
A provider's programmatic interface for calling models directly: a stateless request carrying messages, system prompt and tool definitions, returning generated content plus a usage report, billed per token.

Also known as
fundamentalsAPImodel APIinference API

Why it exists
A CLI and a chat UI both hide the knobs that production needs - which model, what temperature, which tools, how many tokens, what it cost. The API is the surface where those choices are explicit and scriptable.

How it works
You POST messages to a versioned endpoint with a model id, an API key and an anthropic-version header, and receive generated content blocks plus a usage object reporting what the request consumed. Everything in the request counts toward the context window: the system prompt, every message including tool results and images, and your tool definitions. Limits are enforced at the organisation level as rate limits (requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute) and as monthly spend limits, using a token bucket, with a 429 and a retry-after header on breach.

Example
A structured extraction request posts the input plus an output_config.format JSON schema; the response returns text matching that schema, and its usage object reports the exact input and output tokens so the caller can enforce its own budget.

When to use it
Use the API when you need model choice, structured output, programmatic tool definitions, or usage you can bill and monitor. Use a CLI when a person is driving and a harness is enough. Do not build on the API when a single call with good context already solves the task.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

An API is the **raw programmatic surface**: you send messages, tools and a schema; you get content back plus an exact usage report.

Why it exists

Every decision a product makes about model behaviour - which model, which tools, what shape the output, what it may spend - has to live somewhere an application can control. A chat interface hard-codes those. An API exposes them.

How it works

A request carries a model id, an API key, a version header, a system prompt, a list of messages, and optional tool definitions. The response carries generated content blocks and a usage object reporting exactly what the request consumed.

The mechanics that shape your design:

**Everything counts.** The docs are explicit that the system prompt, every message - including tool results, images and documents - and your tool definitions all count toward the context window, as does the generated output including extended thinking.

**Usage is reported, not estimated.** Every response reports consumption in its `usage` field, which is what makes per-feature cost attribution possible.

**Limits are enforced.** Rate limits are measured in requests per minute, input tokens per minute and output tokens per minute, per model class. Spend limits cap monthly cost. Both use a token bucket, so capacity replenishes continuously rather than resetting on a clock, and a breach returns 429 with a `retry-after` header.

 Rate limits can bite harder than the nominal per-minute number. The docs note that a limit of 60 RPM may be enforced as 1 request per second, so a short burst can exceed the limit even when the average looks compliant. 

When to use it

Use the API when you need model selection, structured output, programmatic tools, or usage you can attribute and budget. Prefer a CLI when a person is driving and a harness already covers it.

Do not reach for the API to solve a problem a single call with good context already solves. Anthropic's guidance is to find the simplest solution and only add complexity when needed.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not MCP"> An API is system-specific and usually needs bespoke code per caller. MCP is a shared contract for AI applications, so one server serves many clients. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a CLI"> The API exposes model, tools and format as explicit parameters. A CLI has already chosen most of them for you. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a tool"> A tool is one capability defined inside a request. The API is the channel it travels on, plus the model call. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a harness"> The harness is loop, tools, permissions and context policy. The API gives you the model call; you assemble the rest. </Accordion>

Example

A structured extraction request posts the input plus an `output_config.format` JSON schema. The response returns text matching that schema and a `usage` object with exact token counts, so the caller can both parse the result deterministically and enforce a per-request budget.

Related concepts

- Token - the unit the API bills and limits in
- Structured outputs - schema-constrained responses
- Tool - the capabilities defined per request

body:
Definition
A command-line interface for driving an AI agent - a program that takes a prompt and flags on stdin and produces text, JSON, or an exit code, so the same surface serves an interactive developer and an automated pipeline.

Also known as
toolingcommand-line interfacecli-firstterminal agent

Why it exists
Agents have to be usable in two places: by a person typing at a terminal, and by CI running unattended. A GUI serves the first and fails the second. A CLI serves both, composes with shell pipelines, and gives automation an exit status to branch on.

How it works
The CLI wraps the harness and exposes its controls as flags. Claude Code's reference documents `claude` to start an interactive session, `claude -p` to query non-interactively then exit, `claude -c` to continue, and `claude -r` to resume by id or name - plus `--allowedTools`, `--output-format`, and flags that conflict explicitly, such as --bg and --cloud with a task. Exit codes carry the result: 0 on success, non-zero on failure.

Example
The same agent, two surfaces: `claude 'explain this project'` for a developer at a terminal, and `claude -p 'Find and fix the bug in auth.py' --allowedTools 'Read,Edit,Bash'` in a CI step, which exits 0 or non-zero so the pipeline can branch.

When to use it
Use a CLI when a human drives it, when it must run in CI, or when output needs to be piped or captured. Use a library SDK when the calling program needs structured message objects, tool-approval callbacks, or fine-grained control rather than a process boundary.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A CLI is the agent's **process boundary**: strings in, exit code out. That is exactly what makes it work for a developer at a terminal and for CI.

Why it exists

Two callers, one tool. A person wants a prompt box, a transcript, and a way to interrupt. A pipeline wants no UI, machine-readable output, and a non-zero exit on failure. A CLI is the one interface that satisfies both without maintaining two products - and it composes with everything else on the machine.

How it works

The CLI is a front end onto the harness, exposing its controls as flags.

CommandWhat it does
`claude`Start an interactive session
`claude "query"`Interactive session seeded with a prompt
`claude -p "query"`Query non-interactively, then exit
`claude -c`Continue the most recent conversation in this directory
`claude -r "" "query"`Resume a session by id or name

Three properties worth relying on:

**Exit codes carry the result.** Claude Code exits 0 on success and non-zero when the run fails, so a script can branch on status rather than parsing prose. An invalid flag is reported to stderr before the run starts.

**`--output-format` carries structure.** When the next step is a program, ask for JSON rather than scraping markdown.

**Conflicts are named, not silent.** Not every flag combines with `-p`; Claude Code rejects incompatible combinations with an error that names the conflict.

 `--bare` is the flag to know about if you script this. It skips auto-discovery of hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, auto memory and CLAUDE.md, so a run produces the same result on every machine. Without it, a hook in a teammate's home directory or an MCP server in the project config can change your CI result. 

When to use it

Use the CLI when a human drives the agent, when it runs in CI or a script, or when output must be captured and piped. Reach for an SDK instead when your program needs structured message objects, tool-approval callbacks, or native streaming objects rather than text across a process boundary.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not an SDK"> The CLI is a process boundary - strings in, text and an exit code out. An SDK is an in-process library returning structured message objects with callbacks. Finer control, tighter coupling. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not the harness"> The CLI is one interface to the harness. The harness is the runtime behind it. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a hook"> A hook fires automatically at an event. A CLI is invoked deliberately, by a person or a script. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not an MCP client"> The CLI is how you talk to the agent. An MCP client is the component inside that agent that talks to MCP servers. </Accordion>

Example

`claude -p "Find and fix the bug in auth.py" --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash" --bare` runs unattended, auto-approves exactly three tools, and exits non-zero on failure. Add `--output-format json` and the result is machine-readable without a parser.

Related concepts

- Harness - the runtime behind the CLI
- API - the programmatic surface
- Hook - events that fire without you invoking anything

frontmatter.title: Context Engineering
frontmatter.description: Curating which tokens enter the model's context window on every turn, and why it superseded prompt engineering as the frame.

body:
Definition
The practice of deciding, on every model call, which tokens enter the context window — system prompt, tools, retrieved data, message history — to maximise signal rather than volume.

Also known as
promptingcontext engineeringcontext management

Why it exists
Anthropic treats context as a critical but finite resource, and notes that accuracy and recall degrade as token count grows (context rot). Prompt engineering optimises one artefact written once; real systems must answer what to include on every single turn, from sources no single author controls.

How it works
The recurring strategies are selection and isolation rather than volume: write durable facts to files read on demand; load content progressively, as skills do with their three-level disclosure; isolate bulky exploration in a subagent so the main window stays clean; compact or clear history for long-running work; and curate the tool set, since every tool definition occupies context.

Example
A naive agent answering why login is slow on staging pulls six logs into the main window, so every later turn carries them and the answer competes with tens of thousands of tokens of noise. An engineered version delegates the log reading to a subagent and keeps the three-sentence finding.

When to use it
Whenever behaviour spans more than one turn — an agent, a long conversation, or any system with retrieval or many tools. For a single self-contained request, a good prompt is enough.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Context engineering is the discipline of deciding, at every step, which tokens go into the model's context window — the system prompt, the tools, the retrieved data, the message history — so that the highest-signal possible set is in front of the model.

Why it exists

Anthropic's framing is that context is a **critical but finite resource**, and that more context is not automatically better. Their own context-window documentation names the failure mode directly: as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade — "context rot".

Prompt engineering optimises one artefact: the words of the prompt. Context engineering generalises it. Anthropic's engineering post describes the shift as building less about "finding the right words and phrases" and more about answering "what configuration of context is most likely to generate our model's desired behavior?" — a question you must answer on every single call, not once at design time.

 The distinction is one of timing and scope. A prompt is written once. Context is assembled on every turn, from sources no single author controls. 

How it works

The recurring strategies, all of which are about *selection and isolation* rather than volume:

- **Write it down.** Put durable facts in files the agent reads on demand instead of

carrying them permanently in the system prompt.

- **Load on demand.** This is what skills do with their three-level progressive disclosure:

the description is always present, the body only when relevant, the supporting files only when referenced.

- **Isolate.** A subagent burns its own context on exploration so the main window stays

clean — the single highest-leverage technique when a task would otherwise flood the main conversation.

- **Compress and clear.** Server-side compaction is the primary strategy for long-running

conversations and agentic workflows, per the context-window documentation.

- **Curate what the tools expose.** Every tool definition sits in the context window, so a

sprawling tool set is a context cost, not just a selection risk.

When to use it

Whenever behaviour depends on more than one turn: an agent, a long conversation, any system with retrieval or many tools. For a single self-contained request, writing a good prompt is still all you need.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not prompt engineering"> Prompt engineering optimises the instruction text you write. Context engineering governs everything else that enters the window — tools, history, retrieved data — and does so on every turn rather than once. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not the context window"> The window is a fixed capacity, a constraint. Context engineering is the practice of deciding what fills it. A million-token window does not remove the need to choose. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not memory"> Memory is one source that may be injected. Context engineering is the broader selection that decides whether it, and what else, is in front of the model this turn. </Accordion>

Example

A naive agent answering "why is login slow on staging?" pulls six logs into the main window. Now every subsequent turn carries those logs, and the answer about login competes with 40,000 tokens of noise. An engineered version delegates the log reading to a subagent, keeps the three-sentence finding, and leaves the window free.

- Sub-agent — isolation in practice
- Skill — load-on-demand in practice

title: Context Window
description: The bounded, per-request working memory of a model — everything it can reference when producing a response.
summary: The bounded, per-request working memory of a model — everything it can reference when producing a response.

frontmatter.title: Context Window
frontmatter.description: The bounded, per-request working memory of a model — everything it can reference when producing a response.

body:
Definition
The total set of text a model can reference when generating a response, including the response itself. It counts the system prompt, every message including tool results and images, the tool definitions you supplied, and the output produced for the turn.

Also known as
fundamentalscontext windowcontextworking memory

Why it exists
The window is bounded and per-request, unlike the training corpus which is fixed at training time. Because everything in it is re-sent on every turn, every token added is a permanent tax on the whole conversation.

How it works
Every response reports consumption in its usage field. With prompt caching the input count splits across input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens, all of which count toward the window. Sizes vary by model — the documentation currently lists several Claude models with a 1M-token window where 1M is the default without a beta header, and notes others such as Claude Sonnet 4.5 have 200k. The key behavioural fact is context rot: accuracy and recall degrade as token count grows, so a larger window is capacity rather than a strategy.

Example
A 2,000-token system prompt, thirty tools averaging 300 tokens of definition each (9,000), a 40,000-token retrieved document and a fifty-turn conversation exhaust a smaller window before the model writes a word — and even inside a large one, that document competes with everything else for attention.

When to use it
Treat it as a budget: before adding a tool definition, a retrieved document or a long history, ask what it displaces. For long-running conversations and agentic workflows, server-side compaction is the primary documented strategy.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

The context window is the total set of text a model can reference when producing a response, including the response itself — its working memory, not its training data.

Why it exists

The distinction between the training corpus and the working memory is the one that trips people up. The context window is bounded and per-request; everything in it counts on every turn.

How it works

The documentation is explicit about what counts, which is usually the surprise:

- the system prompt,
- every message in `messages`, including tool results, images and documents,
- **your tool definitions**,
- and the output generated for the turn, including extended thinking.

Every response reports consumption in its `usage` field. With prompt caching the input count splits across `input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens` — and all three count toward the window.

Sizes vary by model. The documentation currently lists a set of Claude models with a 1M-token window, where 1M is the default with no beta header, and notes that other models such as Claude Sonnet 4.5 have a 200k-token window. A single request can include up to 600 images or PDF pages, or 100 for models with a 200k window.

 Model names, sizes and limits change often. Read the current context window page for the numbers; do not trust a cached figure, including one written here. 

The behaviour that matters most: as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade. The official name is **context rot**. This is why a larger window is capacity, not a strategy — more is not automatically better, which is the premise of context engineering.

When to use it

Think of it as a budget. Before adding a tool definition, a retrieved document or a long history, ask what it displaces. For long-running conversations and agentic workflows, the documentation names server-side compaction as the primary strategy for context management.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not memory"> A model's weights encode general knowledge; the context window is per-request working space. Anything you want reliably available must be in the window, or written somewhere the agent reads on demand. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a size to maximise"> Capacity is not quality. Beyond a point, adding tokens degrades accuracy — context rot — so filling the window is not a goal. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not the training data"> The training corpus is orders of magnitude larger and fixed at training time. The window is what you supply on this request. </Accordion>

Example

A system prompt of 2,000 tokens, thirty tools averaging 300 tokens of definition each (9,000), a retrieved document of 40,000, and a 50-turn conversation will exhaust a smaller window before the model writes a word — and even inside a large one, that 40,000-token document will be competing with everything else for attention.

Related concepts

- Context engineering — deciding what fills it
- Sub-agent — spending context somewhere else
- Tool — definitions that silently consume it

title: Embedding

summary: A vector representation of text or media that encodes meaning so similar items land close together - the machinery under semantic search and retrieval.

frontmatter.title: Embedding
frontmatter.description: A vector representation of text or media that encodes meaning so similar items land close together - the machinery under semantic search and retrieval.

body:
Definition
A fixed-length vector produced from text or media that encodes semantic meaning, so that inputs with similar meaning have vectors close together and can be found by similarity search.

Also known as
retrievalembeddingsvector representationvector embedding

Why it exists
Keyword search fails when the query uses different words than the document. Embeddings let you match on meaning instead of lexical overlap, which is what makes semantic search and RAG retrieval work at all.

How it works
An embedding model maps text to a vector of numbers such that semantic similarity is reflected as geometric proximity. Retrieval embeds the query and searches the stored vectors for nearest neighbours. pgvector, for example, stores vectors alongside other Postgres data and supports L2, inner product, cosine, L1, Hamming and Jaccard distance, with exact and approximate nearest-neighbour search.

Example
A user asks 'how do I cancel?' against a corpus whose article is titled 'Ending your subscription early'. No keyword overlap survives, but the embeddings are close, so the article is retrieved.

When to use it
Use embeddings for semantic search, retrieval, deduplication, clustering, and recommendation. Do not use them when exact-match lookup suffices - a SQL equality check is faster, cheaper and exact. Do not compare embeddings produced by different models against each other.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

An embedding is a vector that encodes **meaning**, so similarity can be measured geometrically instead of by matching words.

Why it exists

Keyword search requires overlap. "How do I cancel?" and "Ending your subscription early" share almost no tokens and answer the same question. Embeddings exist so that pair can be matched.

How it works

An embedding model maps text to a vector such that semantic similarity becomes geometric proximity. Retrieval embeds the query, then searches the stored vectors for nearest neighbours.

pgvector is a useful concrete example of the storage side: it stores vectors alongside other Postgres data and supports exact and approximate nearest-neighbour search across several distance functions - L2, inner product, cosine, L1, Hamming, Jaccard - over single-precision, half-precision, binary and sparse vectors.

 Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval adds a step before embedding: each chunk is prefixed with a short generated description of the document it came from. Chunks that lose their context when split - a table of rates separated from the heading that explains them - become retrievable again. Reported effect: 49% fewer failed retrievals, 67% with reranking. 

When to use it

Use embeddings when you need meaning-based matching: semantic search, RAG retrieval, deduplication, clustering, recommendations, or routing a query to a specialist handler.

Do not use them when exact match suffices - an indexed equality check is faster, cheaper and correct. Do not mix embedding spaces: vectors from different models are not comparable.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not a token"> A token is a unit of text a model reads. An embedding is a fixed-length vector representing meaning - a different representation. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a vector database"> An embedding is the vector. A vector database indexes embeddings and answers similarity queries over them. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not RAG"> RAG is the full pipeline. Embeddings are the comparison mechanism inside its retrieval step. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a generative model"> An embedding model is trained to produce vectors, not text. Fine-tuning a generative model does not give you an embedding model. </Accordion>

Example

A user asks "how do I cancel?" against a corpus whose article is titled "Ending your subscription early". There is no keyword overlap worth relying on, but the two embeddings are close, so the article is retrieved.

Related concepts

- Vector database - storing and searching embeddings
- RAG - the pipeline embeddings serve

title: Eval
description: A repeatable test for an AI system: give it an input, apply grading logic to its output, and measure success against criteria you defined in advance.
summary: A repeatable test for an AI system: give it an input, apply grading logic to its output, and measure success against criteria you defined in advance.

frontmatter.title: Eval
frontmatter.description: A repeatable test for an AI system: give it an input, apply grading logic to its output, and measure success against criteria you defined in advance.

body:
Definition
A repeatable test for an AI system - one input, one output, and grading logic that scores it against defined success criteria - structured as tasks, trials and graders so results are comparable across runs.

Also known as
evaluationevalevaluationevalsgrading

Why it exists
Without evals you notice problems in production, where fixing one failure creates others. Anthropic's framing: evals make problems and behavioural changes visible before they reach users, and their value compounds over an agent's lifecycle. For prompts specifically, success criteria and evals are described as central to prompt engineering rather than an afterthought.

How it works
An eval is a prompt or task, a response, and grading logic. For agent systems the structure is richer: a task is a single test with defined inputs and success criteria; each attempt is a trial, run multiple times because model output varies; a grader scores some aspect of performance, and a task can have multiple graders. Anthropic's agent evals use unit tests as graders - a coding agent is asked to build an MCP server, and grading verifies the working server rather than judging prose.

Example
Criteria stated as measurable rather than vague: instead of 'classifies sentiment well', set 'achieves F1 of at least 0.85 on a held-out set of 10,000 diverse posts, a 5% improvement over the current baseline'. That number can fail.

When to use it
Use evals before you change anything, not after - a prompt edit, a model swap, a new tool. For agents, run several trials per task, because a single run measures noise as much as capability. Do not build a large eval suite before you have success criteria; the criteria are the hard part.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

An eval is a **repeatable test**: input in, output graded against criteria you wrote down beforehand.

Why it exists

Reactive debugging in production is the failure mode evals exist to prevent. Anthropic's argument: without them you catch issues only once users do, where fixing one failure creates others. Evals make problems and behavioural changes visible early, and the value compounds the longer an agent lives.

How it works

Simplest form: a prompt, a response, and grading logic.

Agent systems need more structure, and Anthropic defines it precisely:

TermWhat it is
**Task**One test with defined inputs and success criteria
**Trial**One attempt at that task - run several, because output varies between runs
**Grader**Logic scoring some aspect of performance; a task can have several

For a coding agent, the grader is often a unit test: hand the agent "build an MCP server", let it run its loop, then grade by verifying the working server.

 Agents are harder to evaluate precisely because the same capabilities that make them useful

- autonomy, many turns, adapting to intermediate results - let mistakes propagate. And a

capable model can find a solution the eval never anticipated: Anthropic notes Opus 4.5 solved a flight-booking benchmark by discovering a policy loophole, technically failing the eval as written while serving the user better. 

When to use it

Use evals before every change - prompt edit, model swap, new tool, new retrieval step. Run multiple trials per task for agents. Use unit-test graders where the output is code.

Write the success criteria before the eval harness. Anthropic's criteria are specific and measurable: not "classifies sentiment well" but "F1 of at least 0.85 on a held-out set of 10,000 diverse posts, a 5% improvement over the current baseline". Only the second can fail.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not evaluation"> An eval is one repeatable test. Evaluation is the discipline of building and maintaining a set of them and acting on the results. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a unit test"> A unit test asserts a deterministic expected value. An eval grades output that legitimately varies between runs, which is why it needs trials. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not observability"> Observability reports what happened in production. An eval says whether it was good, and can run in CI before deployment. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not prompting"> Prompting is the craft of improving a prompt. An eval is how you learn whether the improvement worked. </Accordion>

Example

Instead of "classifies sentiment well", set: F1 of at least 0.85 on a held-out set of 10,000 diverse posts, five percent above the current baseline. That is specific, measurable, relevant and achievable - and it can fail, which is the point.

Related concepts

- Evaluation - the discipline around evals
- Observability - what happened in production

title: Evaluation
description: Defining measurable success criteria for an LLM feature and building a test set that measures them, so quality claims are evidence.
summary: Defining measurable success criteria for an LLM feature and building a test set that measures them, so quality claims are evidence.

frontmatter.title: Evaluation
frontmatter.description: Defining measurable success criteria for an LLM feature and building a test set that measures them, so quality claims are evidence.

body:
Definition
The practice of defining what good means for an LLM feature in specific, measurable terms and building evaluations that measure performance against them — turning quality claims into evidence.

Also known as
fundamentalsevaluationevalsevaltesting LLMs

Why it exists
LLM output is non-deterministic and subjective, which makes eyeballing twenty outputs an unreliable way to detect change. Without a measurement loop you cannot distinguish an improvement from a coincidence, so every later change is a gamble.

How it works
Define criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant — 'F1 of at least 0.85 on a held-out set of 10,000 diverse posts, a 5% improvement over baseline' rather than 'classifies well'. Choose a measurement method: quantitative metrics, qualitative scales and rubrics, A/B testing against a baseline to catch regressions, and edge-case analysis to catch what the happy path hides. Hold out a test set the system was not tuned on, or you measure memorisation rather than capability.

Example
A summarisation feature judged by reading twenty outputs shows improvement both when you changed something and when you did nothing, because samples are noisy. Scoring the same twenty against a defined rubric — factual consistency, coverage of required points, no invented content — makes the comparison meaningful and repeatable.

When to use it
Before shipping anything whose quality will be asked about, and always before claiming an improvement. If you cannot state your criteria, you do not know whether you have them.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Evaluation is the practice of defining what "good" means for an LLM feature in measurable terms, then building a test set that measures it — so that claims about quality are evidence, not opinion.

Why it exists

Because LLM output is non-deterministic and subjective, and both of those make it suspicious to eyeball. The official documentation's framing is a cycle at the centre of prompt engineering: define your success criteria, build evaluations, improve against the failures, re-measure.

Without that loop you cannot tell an improvement from a coincidence, which makes every subsequent change a gamble.

How it works

**Define criteria that are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant.** The documentation shows the transformation, and the example is the part worth remembering:

Criteria
Bad"The model should classify sentiments well"
GoodF1 ≥ 0.85 on a held-out set of 10,000 diverse posts, a 5% improvement over baseline

"Safe outputs" is not a criterion. "Fewer than 0.1% of outputs out of 10,000 trials flagged for toxicity by the content filter" is.

**Choose a measurement method.** Quantitative metrics (F1, accuracy, precision, recall; operational measures like response time), or qualitative scales (Likert, expert rubrics). A/B testing against a baseline catches regressions. Edge-case analysis catches the cases your happy path hides.

**Hold out a test set** the system was not tuned on, or you have measured memorisation rather than capability.

 The documentation also sets a boundary worth internalising: not every failure is a prompt failure. Latency and cost can often be improved more easily by choosing a different model than by engineering the prompt further. 

When to use it

Before shipping anything whose quality you will be asked about, and always before claiming an improvement. If you cannot state your criteria, you cannot know whether you have them.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not unit tests"> Code tests assert that a function returns a specific value. Evaluations measure a distribution of outputs against criteria — no single expected answer usually exists. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not prompting"> Evaluation measures; prompting changes what is measured. Neither replaces the other: an improved prompt with no eval is unverified, an eval with no improvement is instrumentation you do not act on. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a quality guarantee"> An eval measures a distribution on a test set. A model can score well on it and still fail in production on inputs unlike anything you held out. </Accordion>

Example

A summarisation feature judged by reading twenty outputs will show improvement when you changed something and will also show it when you did nothing, because samples are noisy. Scoring the same twenty against a defined rubric — factual consistency, coverage of required points, no invented content — makes the comparison meaningful and repeatable.

Related concepts

- Prompting — what the evaluation loop improves
- Hallucination — a rate you can actually measure
- Structured outputs — removes parsing noise from eval

title: Guardrails
description: The policy and permission layer that constrains what an agent may do - read-only by default, explicit approval for writes, scoped roots and denied tools.
summary: The policy and permission layer that constrains what an agent may do - read-only by default, explicit approval for writes, scoped roots and denied tools.

frontmatter.title: Guardrails
frontmatter.description: The policy and permission layer that constrains what an agent may do - read-only by default, explicit approval for writes, scoped roots and denied tools.

body:
Definition
The policy and permission layer around an agent - default-deny on side effects, explicit approval for sensitive operations, scoped directories, and tool-level allow or deny - that bounds what a run can affect.

Also known as
safetyguardrailspermissionssafety railsleast privilege

Why it exists
An agent that can edit files, run commands and call external systems can cause real damage from a wrong guess or an injected instruction. Guardrails move the boundary from trusting the model's judgement to enforcing it in the host.

How it works
Claude Code is the concrete reference: strict read-only permissions by default, with additional actions - editing files, running tests, executing commands - requiring explicit permission. A built-in set of read-only commands such as ls, cat and git status runs without a prompt. MCP servers extend the same boundary: the filesystem server treats the directories you pass as the entire security boundary, resolving paths before access checks so symlinks pointing outside an allowed root are rejected rather than followed.

Example
A coding agent scoped to ~/projects/my-app with the filesystem server mounted on src and docs cannot read .env, .git or node_modules, and any destructive bash command requires explicit approval. Testing the negative case - asking it to read a file just outside the root - takes ten seconds and tells you more than reading the config.

When to use it
Use guardrails by default for any agent with side effects. Scope file access to the project, not the home directory. Pre-approve read-only tools and require approval for writes. Do not rely on the model to respect boundaries - enforce them in the host.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Guardrails are the layer that says **no** on the model's behalf: read-only by default, explicit approval for writes, scoped roots, denied tools.

 The principle: a request in a prompt is a request. A guardrail is enforced by the host no matter what the model decides. Only the second one holds when the model is wrong. 

Why it exists

An agent with file, shell and network access can do real damage from a wrong guess - or from an instruction it read in a document. Guardrails move the safety boundary out of the model's judgement and into the host, where it is deterministic.

How it works

Claude Code is the concrete reference implementation:

- **Read-only by default.** Strict read-only permissions until more is requested.
- **Explicit approval for side effects.** Editing files, running tests, executing commands

each require permission; the user chooses approve-once or allow-automatically.

- **Allow-list for safe reads.** Built-in read-only commands - ls, cat, git status - run

without a prompt.

MCP servers extend the boundary rather than bypass it. The filesystem server's design is worth copying: the directories you pass are the entire security boundary, there is no "allow everything" flag, and paths are resolved before access checks so a symlink pointing outside an allowed root is rejected rather than followed.

For network-facing servers, the MCP specification's security guidance adds: validate the Origin header on incoming connections to prevent DNS rebinding, bind to localhost only when running locally, and implement proper authentication.

When to use it

Always, for any agent with side effects. Specifically:

- Scope file servers to the project, not the home directory.
- Mount `src` and `docs` rather than the repo root, so `.env` and `.git` are unreachable.
- Pre-approve read-only tools; require approval for writes and network calls.
- Test the negative case: ask the agent to read something outside its boundary and confirm

the call fails.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not a hook"> A hook is one mechanism a guardrail can be built from. A guardrail is the policy; PreToolUse is an enforcement point. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not prompt injection"> Prompt injection is the attack. Guardrails are the defences - permissions, scoped roots, denied tools. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a sandbox"> A sandbox is isolation at the OS or container level. A guardrail is policy expressed as permissions; a sandbox is one way to make it real. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a prompt"> Asking the model in a prompt to be careful is a request. A guardrail is enforced regardless of what the model decides. </Accordion>

Example

A coding agent scoped to `~/projects/my-app`, with the filesystem server mounted on `src` and `docs`, cannot reach `.env`, `.git` or `node_modules` - and any destructive bash command requires explicit approval. Asking it to read a file just outside the root should fail, and confirming that takes ten seconds.

Related concepts

- Hook - where guardrails get enforced
- Prompt injection - the threat they mitigate

title: Hallucination
description: Fluent, confident output that is not supported by fact — and the mitigations that actually reduce it.
summary: Fluent, confident output that is not supported by fact — and the mitigations that actually reduce it.

frontmatter.title: Hallucination
frontmatter.description: Fluent, confident output that is not supported by fact — and the mitigations that actually reduce it.

body:
Definition
Output that is fluent and plausible but unsupported — a fabricated fact, a non-existent citation, or an invented API detail. Anthropic's documentation states that even advanced models can generate text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with the given context.

Also known as
model-behaviorhallucinationconfabulation

Why it exists
The training objective rewards plausible text, and plausibility is not truth. When a question requires a fact the model lacks, the pressure to answer fluently persists. It also surfaces outside the model: an empty search result, a failing tool, or a retrieval pipeline returning the wrong document all produce confident wrong output.

How it works
The official mitigation strategy is to make the ground truth reachable and mandatory: give explicit permission to say 'I don't know'; extract verbatim quotes before analysing long documents; require a supporting quote per claim and retract claims without one; inspect summarised reasoning when an answer looks wrong; and run best-of-N to surface inconsistency. Each technique forces the answer to be anchored to retrievable text rather than to fluency.

Example
Asked about a function that does not exist in the codebase, a model will still write a plausible implementation. Giving it tools to look up the symbol and instructing it to admit failure converts a confident fabrication into an honest negative result, which is strictly more useful.

When to use it
Whenever being wrong costs more than admitting ignorance — research, factual Q&A over private data, anything that reaches a user as a claim. Not the right frame for creative or open-ended work.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A hallucination is output that is fluent and plausible but not actually supported — a fabricated fact, a citation that does not exist, or an API detail invented with total confidence.

Why it exists

The objective is to produce plausible text. Plausibility and truth are different things, and nothing in the training objective makes the second one automatic. When a question requires a fact the model does not have, the pressure to produce a fluent answer still applies — so it produces one.

Anthropic's own documentation states this plainly: "Even the most advanced language models, like Claude, can sometimes generate text that is factually incorrect or inconsistent with the given context."

 Hallucination is not only about models inventing facts. It is also about **retrieval and tool systems**: a search that returns nothing, a tool that errors, or a retrieval pipeline that returns the wrong document will all produce confident-sounding wrong output. Sometimes the fix is in your pipeline, not the model. 

How it works

The official mitigation guide is built around one idea: **make the ground truth reachable and mandatory**. Its techniques, roughly in order of strength:

- **Allow "I don't know."** Give explicit permission to admit uncertainty. The guide calls

this out as a basic strategy that can drastically reduce false information — and it is by far the cheapest.

- **Ground with direct quotes.** For long documents, have the model extract verbatim quotes

first and base the analysis on those only.

- **Require citations, and retract without them.** Draft the answer, then for each claim find

a supporting quote. If no quote exists, the claim must be removed and the removal marked.

- **Check the reasoning.** Use thinking with summarised display and read the summary when an

answer looks wrong — faulty logic is often visible before the conclusion.

- **Best-of-N.** Run the same prompt several times and compare. Inconsistency across runs is

a signal that the content is not solid.

When to use it

Any task where being wrong is more expensive than admitting ignorance: research, factual Q&A over private data, anything that reaches a user as a claim. For open-ended or creative work, "hallucination" is not the right frame.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not the same as uncertainty"> The model can state its uncertainty and still be wrong. "I am not sure" is a behaviour to design for, not proof of correctness. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a formatting error"> Structured output guarantees a shape, not a true content. A perfectly schema-valid JSON object can be entirely fabricated — see structured outputs. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not fixed by more context"> Past a certain size, longer context degrades accuracy (context rot) rather than reducing hallucination. Retrieval quality matters more than retrieval quantity. </Accordion>

Example

Asked about a function that does not exist in the codebase, a model will still write a plausible implementation. Giving it tools to *look up* the symbol, and instructing it to say "I don't know" when the lookup fails, converts a confident fabrication into an honest negative — which is strictly more useful.

summary: The runtime around a model - the loop, tools, permissions and context management that turn a model into a usable agent.

frontmatter.title: Harness
frontmatter.description: The runtime around a model - the loop, tools, permissions and context management that turn a model into a usable agent.

body:
Definition
The runtime wrapped around a model - the agent loop, tool set, permission model, context management and stopping conditions. The harness is what you are actually talking to when you use an agentic product.

Also known as
agentsagent harnessagentic harness

Why it exists
A model emits tokens. Everything that makes an agent useful - which tools exist, what needs approval, what stays in context, when to stop - is engineered outside the weights. Naming that layer separately makes it swappable: the same harness can drive a different model.

How it works
The harness owns the loop and everything around it. Anthropic describes the Agent SDK as giving the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code, and calls the default Claude Code harness built for coding. A harness also decides orchestration shape: Anthropic documents harness patterns such as classify-and-act, fan-out-and-synthesize, adversarial verification, generate-and-filter, tournament, and loop-until-done.

Example
The default Claude Code harness plans and executes in one context window, which works for most coding tasks. For a flaky test that fails 1 in 50 runs, the documented approach is a workflow: separate subagents each with their own context window, competing theories about the race, stopping when one survives the evidence.

When to use it
Reach for harness-level thinking when a task class breaks down under the default loop - long-running, massively parallel, heavily structured or adversarial work. Do not build a custom harness when a single model call with good context already solves the task.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A harness is the runtime around a model: the loop, the tools, the permissions, the context policy. It is the difference between "a model that can answer" and "a system you can hand a repository to".

 Model + harness = agent. Most confusion in this area is a missing word. "Claude did it" usually means the harness did it, using Claude. 

Why it exists

Model behaviour is mostly fixed at training time. Product behaviour is not. Which tools exist, what a user must approve, how much history survives a compaction, when the loop stops - none of that lives in the weights. All of it lives in the harness.

Giving the layer its own name pays off twice: engineers can reason about "the model got this wrong" versus "the harness fed it the wrong context", and the harness can be pointed at a different model without rewriting the product.

How it works

The harness owns the loop and the policy around it.

Anthropic describes the Agent SDK as providing "the same tools, agent loop, and context management that power Claude Code" - so the SDK is the supported way to embed that runtime in your own application, in Python or TypeScript.

Anthropic also calls the default Claude Code harness *built for coding*, while noting it is useful more broadly because many tasks resemble coding tasks. The classes where the default harness does not reach peak performance are research, security analysis, agent teams and code review - the cases where planning and executing in a single context window breaks down.

The patterns Anthropic documents for those cases are harness patterns:

PatternWhat the harness does
Classify-and-actA classifier agent routes the task to different agents
Fan-out-and-synthesizeMany agents each get a clean context, one merges the results
Adversarial verificationA second spawned agent tries to refute each result
Generate-and-filterGenerate candidates, filter by rubric, dedupe
TournamentN agents compete on the same task, a judge picks pairwise winners
Loop until doneKeep spawning until a stop condition, not a fixed count

A harness may also choose per-agent model and isolation - Anthropic notes dynamic workflows can decide which models an agent uses and whether subagents run in their own worktree.

When to use it

Reach for harness-level design when a task class breaks the default loop: long-running, massively parallel, heavily structured, or adversarial. Reach for it when you are ranking hundreds of items where one pass would not fit in context.

Do not build a custom harness because a single well-specified model call already solves the task. Anthropic's guidance is to find the simplest solution and only increase complexity when needed - agentic systems trade latency and cost for task performance, and that trade must be worth making.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not a model"> The model is the weights and tokenizer. The harness is the loop, tools, permissions and context policy wrapped around it. Claude Code is a harness; Claude is the model it drives. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not an agent"> An agent is the loop that runs. The harness is the entire runtime hosting that loop plus tools, permissions and context management. One harness hosts many agents. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a workflow"> A workflow is one orchestration pattern defined inside a harness - predefined code paths through LLMs and tools. The harness executes the workflow; it does not define it. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a framework"> A framework is a library that helps you build a harness. The harness is the resulting running system. </Accordion>

Example

The default harness plans and executes in one context window - effective for most coding tasks, and it degrades on a test that fails 1 in 50 runs. The documented fix is a workflow that fans out separate subagents with their own context windows, has them form competing theories about the race, and does not stop until one theory survives the evidence.

Related concepts

- Model - the weights the harness drives
- Workflow - predefined orchestration paths inside a harness
- Orchestration - deciding what runs and in what order
- Hook - deterministic events the harness fires

title: Hook
description: A command, HTTP endpoint or prompt fired automatically at a fixed point in an agent's lifecycle - deterministic where a tool needs a decision.
summary: A command, HTTP endpoint or prompt fired automatically at a fixed point in an agent's lifecycle - deterministic where a tool needs a decision.

frontmatter.title: Hook
frontmatter.description: A command, HTTP endpoint or prompt fired automatically at a fixed point in an agent's lifecycle - deterministic where a tool needs a decision.

body:
Definition
A user-defined shell command, HTTP endpoint or LLM prompt that runs automatically at a specific point in an agent session's lifecycle, matched by event and optionally filtered by a matcher.

Also known as
toolinglifecycle hookhooks

Why it exists
Some actions must happen every time, not when the model chooses to do them. Format code after every edit, notify a human when input is needed, block a dangerous command. Leaving those to the model makes them probabilistic; a hook makes them guaranteed.

How it works
Hooks are declared in a settings file under a hooks block keyed by event name, with a matcher and a list of handlers. Claude Code fires them in three cadences: once per session (SessionStart, SessionEnd), once per turn (UserPromptSubmit, Stop, StopFailure), and on every tool call inside the loop (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, plus PostToolUseFailure and PostToolBatch). Command hooks receive event JSON on stdin; HTTP hooks receive it as the POST body.

Example
A PostToolUse hook with matcher Edit|Write pipes the edited file path from the event JSON into prettier, so every file the model writes is formatted without the model ever deciding to run it.

When to use it
Use hooks for deterministic enforcement - formatting, linting, notifications, permission gates, CI steps. Use them instead of asking the model politely in CLAUDE.md. Do not use a hook for anything needing judgement, where a model-decided tool call fits.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A hook is a command the system runs for you at a fixed point in the session lifecycle, so the action happens every time instead of whenever the model feels like it.

 The Claude Code docs put it plainly: hooks give deterministic control, because certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them. 

Why it exists

Ask a model in CLAUDE.md to always run the formatter, and it usually does - usually. Ask a hook, and it does. The difference between a convention and a guarantee is the whole reason hooks exist.

How it works

You declare hooks in a settings file, keyed by event name, with an optional matcher and one or more handlers:

json
`{ "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "jq -r '.tool_input.file_path' | xargs npx prettier --write" } ] } ] } }`

Claude Code fires events in three cadences:

CadenceEvents
Once per session`SessionStart`, `SessionEnd`
Once per turn`UserPromptSubmit`, `Stop`, `StopFailure`
Every tool call in the loop`PreToolUse`, `PostToolUse`

Command hooks get event JSON on stdin; HTTP hooks get it as the POST body. A handler can inspect the input, act, and return a decision - which is what makes `PreToolUse` a permission gate rather than just a notification.

Three things worth knowing before you rely on this:

- Hooks fire wherever Claude Code runs - terminal, IDE extension, Desktop app, web.
- Matcher semantics matter: `"matcher": ""` means every event of that type.
- Hooks also run in `-p` non-interactive sessions, so a hook can change CI behaviour

without anyone deciding it should.

When to use it

Use hooks when the action must always happen: formatting after edits, linting, notifying a human when the agent needs input, blocking a destructive command, running tests on stop.

Do not use a hook for decisions that need judgement. The docs note you can also use prompt-based or agent-based hooks that call a model to evaluate a condition - but that is a tool call with extra ceremony, and the deterministic version is usually better.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not a tool"> A tool is invoked because the model chose to. A hook fires because a lifecycle event happened. Hooks are deterministic; tools are model-directed. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a skill"> A skill is instructions loaded when relevant - a suggestion the agent may follow. A hook is a rule the system enforces regardless of the agent's judgement. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a sub-agent"> A sub-agent is a delegated worker with its own context. A hook is usually a shell command with no model in the loop at all. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not an MCP server"> An MCP server is a long-lived process exposing capabilities over the protocol. A hook is a short-lived command bound to an event inside one host. </Accordion>

Example

The `PostToolUse` hook above reads `tool_input.file_path` straight out of the event JSON and pipes it to prettier. Every file the model edits gets formatted, and the model was never asked to remember.

Related concepts

- Tool - the model-directed counterpart
- Harness - the runtime firing these events
- Guardrails - the policy hooks help enforce

title: Inference
