frontmatter.title: Inference
frontmatter.description: Running a trained model to produce output - the compute step where prompt in, tokens out, latency and cost are incurred.

body:
Definition
The act of running a trained model against a prompt to generate output. Every call incurs latency, token cost and rate-limit consumption - inference is the phase where those costs are actually paid.

Also known as
fundamentalsinferencemodel inferenceinference time

Why it exists
Training and inference are different phases with different economics. Inference happens on every request, forever, so the levers that matter - which model, how many tokens in and out, how much reasoning - are all inference-time decisions rather than research decisions.

How it works
A prompt is tokenised, the model generates tokens until a stopping condition, and the response reports what it consumed in its usage field. The costs that follow are denominated in tokens: price is published per million input and output tokens, and rate limits are expressed in requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute. Extended thinking changes how many tokens are generated before the answer, and that thinking both costs output tokens and occupies context window.

Example
A classification call at 200 input tokens and 40 output tokens on a cheap model costs almost nothing and returns in well under a second. The same call routed to a frontier model for a task that did not need it spends an order of magnitude more for no measurable quality gain.

When to use it
Think in inference terms when choosing a model, setting a budget, or deciding whether a task deserves a stronger model. The question is always: what quality gain does this price and latency buy on this task?

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Inference is **running** a model. It is the phase where every millisecond and every token of your bill is incurred.

Why it exists

Training and inference have different economics. Training happens once and produces weights. Inference happens on every request, forever - so almost every engineering decision that shows up in a budget or a latency budget is an inference-time decision.

How it works

Prompt in, tokens generated, usage reported. The costs that follow are all denominated in tokens.

- **Price** is published per million input and output tokens, and differs by roughly an

order of magnitude across the model lineup.

- **Rate limits** are measured in requests per minute, input tokens per minute and output

tokens per minute, per model class.

- **Reasoning costs tokens.** Extended thinking generates tokens before the answer; they

are billed as output and they occupy context window.

 Latency is not only a model property. Relative latency across the lineup is explicitly qualified as depending on prompt length, output length and thinking effort - so a "fast model" with a huge prompt can be slower than a slow model with a small one. 

When to use it

Reason in these terms when choosing a model, setting a budget, or deciding whether a task deserves a stronger model. The useful question is concrete: what measurable quality gain does this price and latency buy on this specific task?

Do not assume a stronger model is better. Anthropic's prompting guidance notes that latency and cost can be improved more easily by selecting a different model - model choice is often a bigger lever than prompt rewrites.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not a model"> A model is the artefact. Inference is one occurrence of running it - and one billable event. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not training"> Training produces the weights once. Inference uses them on every request. Different phases, different economics. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a token"> A token is the unit inference moves. Inference is the process. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a rate limit"> A rate limit caps how much inference you may run per minute. The limit throttles this phase. </Accordion>

Example

A classification call at 200 input tokens and 40 output tokens on a fast model costs approximately nothing and returns quickly. Routed to a frontier model for a task that did not need it, the same call spends an order of magnitude more for no measurable gain.

Related concepts

- Model - the artefact being run
- Token - the unit being metered
- Rate limits - the per-minute throttle

title: MCP Client
description: The per-server protocol component inside a host application, and how it differs from the host itself.
summary: The per-server protocol component inside a host application, and how it differs from the host itself.

frontmatter.title: MCP Client
frontmatter.description: The per-server protocol component inside a host application, and how it differs from the host itself.

body:
Definition
A component created by an MCP host that maintains one connection to one MCP server, discovers its capabilities, and relays protocol results back to the host and the model.

Also known as
mcpMCP clientclient

Why it exists
The official guide separates the host from the client deliberately: the host is the application a user interacts with, the client is the protocol-level component that makes a server connection possible. One client per server is what keeps a server's context, credentials and permissions isolated from every other server.

How it works
The host instantiates one client per server with a 1:1 relationship. It speaks JSON-RPC over the server transport, discovers tools/resources/prompts with the list operations, issues tools/call when the model acts, and turns results into model-visible content. Clients also serve servers: elicitation lets a server ask the user for specific information, in form mode or URL mode. Sampling and roots are deprecated as of protocol version 2026-07-28.

Example
Claude Code acting as host creates one client per configured server. The host merges both servers' tool lists into a single flat list for the model, and the model never sees which client a tool arrived through.

When to use it
Write one when you are building an AI application that should consume the existing MCP server ecosystem. Do not write one when you use an existing client such as Claude Code — the client already exists, and you install servers.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

An MCP client is the per-connection protocol component that a host application instantiates to talk to exactly one MCP server — it issues requests and carries results back to the host.

Why it exists

The official client guide draws the distinction explicitly: **the host is the application users interact with, while clients are the protocol-level components that enable server connections.** Without that separation, "the client" is ambiguous — people mean Claude Desktop when they mean the host, and the connection machinery when they mean the client.

How it works

Each host creates one client per server, giving a 1:1 relationship. The client:

- speaks JSON-RPC 2.0 over the server's transport,
- discovers capabilities with `tools/list`, `resources/list`, `prompts/list`,
- issues `tools/call` when the model decides to act,
- converts protocol results into the form the host puts in front of the model,
- keeps the security boundary between servers.

Clients can also provide features *to* servers. The current client guide documents **elicitation** — a server pausing to request specific information from the user, in either form mode (structured data collected through a schema the client renders) or URL mode (the user goes out of band, and the data never passes through the client).

 One clarification that matters when you read older tutorials: **sampling** (a server asking the client to run an LLM completion) and **roots** (a client telling a server which directories to focus on) are deprecated as of protocol version `2026-07-28`. They still appear in older code and older guides. 

When to use it

You are writing an MCP client when you are building an AI application that should reach existing servers — then you get an entire ecosystem for free. You are *not* writing one when you use Claude Code or Claude Desktop: they already contain clients, and you install servers.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not the host"> The host is the product — the window, the terminal, the IDE. The client is one internal part per server. Claude Code is the host; the client connecting to your filesystem server lives inside it. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a connector"> The client is code that exists whether or not anyone has configured anything. The connector is the act of pointing a client at a specific server with specific credentials. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a tool"> The client does not execute your business logic. It transports protocol messages and surfaces results; the server executes tools. </Accordion>

Example

Inside a host, connecting two servers creates two clients:

text
`Host (Claude Code) ├── Client 1 ── stdio ──> Server: filesystem └── Client 2 ── HTTP ───> Server: Sentry`

The model sees one flat tool list drawn from both servers, and never learns which client a given tool came through.

Related concepts

- MCP — the protocol this component implements
- MCP server — the other half of the connection
- Agent — the host is where an agent actually runs

title: MCP Connector
description: A configured instance of an MCP server in a client, and the network reality of remote connectors on Claude.
summary: A configured instance of an MCP server in a client, and the network reality of remote connectors on Claude.

frontmatter.title: MCP Connector
frontmatter.description: A configured instance of an MCP server in a client, and the network reality of remote connectors on Claude.

body:
Definition
A configured instance in which one MCP server is connected to one client with credentials, permissions and an enabled capability set. A product-surface term, not a protocol term.

Also known as
mcpconnectorcustom connector

Why it exists
Users think in terms of which connectors are on, not which servers are configured. Separating the deployment instance from the server program also makes it possible to talk about revoking access — you disconnect a connector without uninstalling anything.

How it works
For a remote connector on Claude, the connection to your MCP server is initiated from Anthropic's cloud infrastructure rather than your device, across claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork and the mobile apps, so the server must be reachable over the public internet from Anthropic's IP ranges. A server on a private network behind a VPN or firewall will not connect even if your own machine reaches it. Local servers configured inside Claude Desktop are a separate mechanism. Anthropic warns that custom connectors connect Claude to services it has not verified.

Example
Adding a remote Sentry MCP server as a connector: the user authorises it once, the connection is held from Anthropic's infrastructure rather than the laptop, the server's tools become visible to the model, and the connector can be disconnected later without uninstalling the server.

When to use it
When a remote MCP server already exists for the system you need. Building your own connector is only worth it when nothing suitable exists.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

An MCP connector is a **configured instance**: one remote MCP server wired into one client with credentials, permissions and a set of exposed capabilities.

Why it exists

The word is doing a specific job in product surfaces, and it is worth being precise about it. Anthropic's help centre frames custom connectors as the feature that "let you connect Claude directly to the tools and data sources that matter most to your workflows" — and defines them as the path to connecting an existing remote MCP server, or building your own.

It is a deployment concept, not a protocol concept. MCP does not define connectors. The product surfaces do, because users think in terms of "which connectors are on?", not "which servers are configured?"

How it works

Two things matter in practice, and both are easy to get wrong.

**Who initiates the connection.** For a remote connector on Claude, the connection to your MCP server comes from Anthropic's cloud infrastructure, not from your device — across claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork and the mobile apps. Your server therefore must be reachable over the public internet from Anthropic's IP ranges. A server on a private network behind a VPN or firewall will not connect even when you can reach it from your own machine. Local MCP servers configured inside Claude Desktop are a separate mechanism.

**What the connector exposes.** Custom connectors let Claude operate inside software you connect; the help centre warns explicitly that they connect Claude to services not verified by Anthropic, and that once connected Claude can access those services and take action in them.

 Every server is a program with your data access. Treat adding a connector to a third-party service the way you would treat granting a new integration OAuth scopes: check who runs it and what it can reach. 

When to use it

Use a connector when a remote MCP server already exists for the system you need. Write one yourself only when you have to — most people never do, because most systems now have somebody else's server.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not an MCP server"> The server is the program. The connector is that program, installed and pointed at something. You can install one server in five clients; each installation is a connector. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a plugin"> A plugin is a bundle that can ship MCP server configuration among other things (skills, agents, hooks). A connector is the live connection itself. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not an API key"> The connector is the wiring. The credential is one part of it — the endpoint, the permissions and the enabled capability set are the rest. </Accordion>

Example

Adding a remote Sentry server as a connector: the user authorises it once, Claude's infrastructure holds the connection, the server's tools become visible to the model, and the user can later see which connectors are connected and disconnect them.

Related concepts

- MCP — the protocol behind every connector
- MCP server — the software a connector points at
- MCP client — the component that holds the connection

title: MCP Server
description: The program that implements the server half of MCP, exposes tools and resources, and stays deliberately small.
summary: The program that implements the server half of MCP, exposes tools and resources, and stays deliberately small.

frontmatter.title: MCP Server
frontmatter.description: The program that implements the server half of MCP, exposes tools and resources, and stays deliberately small.

body:
Definition
A program that exposes a focused set of capabilities — tools, resources and prompts — to MCP clients, over stdio or Streamable HTTP, and nothing beyond that scope.

Also known as
mcpMCP serverserver

Why it exists
Because the protocol puts orchestration in the host, a server can be small enough for anyone to write one for a niche system. That is deliberate: the official design principle is that servers should be extremely easy to build, and composability depends on each one staying narrow.

How it works
The server declares capabilities, then serves tools/list and tools/call. Tools carry a name, description and JSON Schema input. Resources are read-only and URI-addressed. The tool list must not vary per connection or as a side effect of other requests, and should be returned in a deterministic order so clients can cache it. stdio transport has the client launch the server as a subprocess and exchange newline-delimited JSON-RPC; Streamable HTTP runs the server independently behind a single POST endpoint.

Example
A GitHub server exposes tools like list_issues and create_pull_request, plus resources for repository metadata. Claude Code runs the client that talks to it; the model sees the tool schemas and issues tool calls the client forwards.

When to use it
Build one when you own a system and want every MCP client to reach it without a per-client integration. Keep it narrow: one server per system beats one server that does everything.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

An MCP server is a program that exposes a focused capability — files, a database, an issue tracker — to AI applications through the MCP protocol, and does nothing else.

Why it exists

The official server guide is blunt about scope: **servers should be extremely easy to build**. All the complex orchestration belongs in the host. That split is what keeps a server small enough that a third party can write one for a niche internal system, and it is why "build a server" is a realistic weekend project rather than a platform effort.

How it works

A server declares its capabilities during setup — for example `{"tools": {"listChanged": true}}` — and then answers two protocol operations:

MethodPurpose
`tools/list`Return the tool definitions with their schemas
`tools/call`Execute one tool with the given arguments

A tool definition is a name, a description, and a JSON Schema for its input. The server returns a result, and the client passes that result back to the model as tool output.

Servers expose the same three primitives — tools, resources, prompts — but most real servers ship only one or two. A filesystem server is tools plus resources. The tool set returned by `tools/list` must not vary per connection or as a side effect of other requests on the same connection, and servers should return tools in a deterministic order so clients can cache the list.

**Transport** decides how the connection is carried:

- **stdio** — the client launches the server as a subprocess and writes newline-delimited

JSON-RPC to its stdin, reading replies from stdout. Local servers usually serve a single client this way.

- **Streamable HTTP** — the server runs independently at one HTTP endpoint handling POST,

with replies returned as JSON or an SSE stream. Remote servers serve many clients this way.

When to use it

Build a server when you own the system and want every MCP client — Claude Code, Claude Desktop, an IDE, your own agent — to reach it without writing an integration per client. Prefer one narrow server per system over one server that does everything; composability is an explicit design goal.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not the MCP protocol"> The protocol is the format. The server is one participant speaking it. Deleting the protocol would break every server; deleting one server breaks one capability in one app. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a tool"> A server is a process; a tool is a named function inside it. One server routinely exposes five tools. Asking "is this a tool or a server?" usually means you are holding a tool definition that a server returned. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a connector"> The server is the software. The connector is the act of installing and configuring it in a client with credentials. You can have five servers and one connector, or one server with five connector instances. </Accordion>

Example

The smallest useful filesystem tool definition a server returns from `tools/list`:

json
`{ "name": "searchFlights", "description": "Search for available flights", "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "origin": { "type": "string", "description": "Departure city" }, "destination": { "type": "string", "description": "Arrival city" }, "date": { "type": "string", "format": "date", "description": "Travel date" } }, "required": ["origin", "destination", "date"] } }`

The model then calls it through the client, which sends `tools/call` on the server's behalf.

Related concepts

- MCP — the protocol the server implements
- MCP client — the other half of every connection
- Tool — what a server actually exposes

frontmatter.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
frontmatter.description: The open protocol for connecting AI applications to external systems, and why it is a protocol rather than a product.

body:
Definition
An open protocol for connecting AI applications to external systems, exchanging context through shared primitives (tools, resources, prompts) over standard transports.

Also known as
mcpModel Context ProtocolMCP

Why it exists
Every AI application previously needed its own custom integration for every data source, so integrations could not be reused across clients. MCP replaces N custom integrations with one agreed wire protocol.

How it works
A host application creates one MCP client per connected MCP server. Servers expose three primitives — tools (model-invoked), resources (application-invoked, read-only, URI-addressed) and prompts (user-invoked templates). Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio or Streamable HTTP. The current protocol revision is 2026-07-28.

Example
A filesystem MCP server exposes tools like read_file and write_file plus resources for files. A host creates one client for it, calls tools/list to discover the tools, puts their schemas in the model's context, and sends tools/call when the model decides to use one.

When to use it
Use MCP when you need an AI application to reach a system it does not natively know — an issue tracker, a database, a design tool, an internal service. Build a server if you own the system and want every MCP client to reach it; consume one if it already exists.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

MCP is a **protocol**: an agreed wire format and vocabulary that lets an AI application connect to external systems without either side inventing a bespoke integration.

The official docs compare it to a USB-C port for AI applications — one connector shape, many devices. Anthropic open-sourced MCP in November 2024 to replace the situation where every AI app wrote a custom integration for every data source.

 MCP is a protocol, not a product. Nobody installs "MCP". You install or build an **MCP server**, and an **MCP client** inside an AI application speaks to it. The current protocol revision is `2026-07-28`; see versioning. 

Why it exists

Before MCP, connecting a model to a system meant writing an adapter in that model's API. An integration written for one assistant could not be reused by another, so the same Jira connection was written three times for three clients.

MCP moves the adapter boundary to a shared, vendor-neutral protocol. The server speaks one language; every MCP-capable client speaks the same language. Anthropic's framing in the launch post: fragmented integrations are replaced by a single protocol.

How it works

Three participants, per the official architecture page:

- **Host** — the AI application the user interacts with (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, an

IDE). It creates clients, holds permissions, and aggregates context.

- **Client** — a per-server protocol component the host instantiates. It maintains exactly

one connection to exactly one server.

- **Server** — a program that exposes capabilities to clients.

Servers expose capabilities through three **primitives**, which differ in who decides to use them:

PrimitiveWhat it isWho initiates
**Tools**A function the model can invoke, with a JSON Schema for its inputThe model
**Resources**Read-only data addressed by URI, supplied as contextThe application
**Prompts**Reusable instruction templates, optionally parameterisedThe user

Messages are JSON-RPC 2.0 over one of two standard transports: **stdio** (the client launches the server as a subprocess and speaks newline-delimited JSON over stdin/stdout) and **Streamable HTTP** (a single MCP endpoint handling POST, with replies returned as a JSON object or a request-scoped SSE stream).

When to use it

Reach for MCP when you want an AI application to read or change data in a system it does not natively know: an issue tracker, a database, a design tool, an internal service. Build a server when you own the system and want every MCP client to reach it; consume a server when someone already built one.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not a plugin"> A plugin is a packaging and distribution mechanism in one host application — a directory containing skills, agents, hooks, or MCP server configurations, with a manifest. MCP is the wire protocol; a plugin is one way to deliver things that use it. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a connector"> A connector is the *installed, configured instance* — the result of wiring a specific MCP server into a specific client with specific credentials. MCP is the standard; a connector is a deployment of a server in an app. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a tool"> MCP is the transport and convention layer. A tool is one callable capability inside it. An MCP server typically exposes several tools; MCP itself is not callable. </Accordion>

Example

A filesystem server exposes two tools and a resource:

json
`{ "name": "read_file", "description": "Read the contents of a file at the given path", "inputSchema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "path": { "type": "string" } }, "required": ["path"] } }`

The client discovers it with `tools/list`, the model decides to call it, and the client sends `tools/call` with `{"name": "read_file", "arguments": {"path": "README.md"}}`.

Related concepts

- MCP server — the program that implements the server half
- MCP client — the per-connection component inside a host
- MCP connector — a configured server instance in an app
- Tool — the callable capability the protocol carries

frontmatter.title: Model
frontmatter.description: The trained weights and tokenizer that predict tokens. Everything that makes an agent useful is engineered around it, not inside it.

body:
Definition
A trained set of weights plus its tokenizer that maps text to tokens and predicts the next token. The model is the reasoning component; it is not an agent, a harness, or an application.

Also known as
fundamentalsLLMlarge language modelmodelfoundation model

Why it exists
Models supply capability: the reasoning, the code knowledge, the instruction following. They deliberately do not supply the things a product needs - a loop, tools, permissions, a place to keep state - because those are deployment decisions that vary per use case.

How it works
Text is tokenised, tokens are embedded, and the model repeatedly predicts a distribution over the next token until a stopping condition. Model identity is a concrete set of published specs, not a vibe: the current Claude lineup publishes an API id, context window, max output, knowledge cutoff, and pricing per million tokens for each model. That published spec is what you select on.

Example
The published lineup makes the trade explicit: Haiku is priced an order of magnitude below Fable and is described for speed; Opus is for complex agentic work; Fable is for demanding reasoning. That is a selection decision made against a spec, not a guess.

When to use it
Choose a model when reasoning quality, context size and cost per token are the binding constraints. Do not expect a model change to fix a context problem, a permissions problem, or a missing tool - those live in the harness.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A model is the trained weights and tokenizer. It predicts tokens. That is the whole of it - and it is not the product.

Why it exists

Models supply capability. Everything else a product needs differs per use case, so it belongs outside the weights. This split is why "upgrade the model" fixes quality problems and never fixes "it forgot what we agreed three turns ago".

How it works

Tokenise the text, embed the tokens, predict a distribution over the next token, repeat until a stopping condition. Extended thinking and effort settings change how much reasoning happens before that answer, and the resulting thinking counts toward the context window.

Model identity is published, not vibes. Each model in the current lineup documents its API id, context window, max output, pricing per million tokens, relative latency, and knowledge cutoff:

Fable 5.1Opus 5Sonnet 5Haiku 4.5
Context window1M1M1M200K
Max output128K128K128K64K
Input $/MTok$10$5$2$1

That table is the selection surface. Pick against it.

 Model ids are pinned snapshots, and aliases move. Always record which id produced a result in your eval logs, or you cannot tell later whether a behaviour change came from the model or from your prompt. 

When to use it

Choose a model when reasoning quality, context size or cost per token is the binding constraint. Switch models when a capability limit is real - a task needs longer reasoning or a bigger window than the current model allows.

Do not switch models expecting it to fix context assembly, a missing tool, or a permissions gap. Those are harness problems.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not an agent"> The model reasons and emits tokens. The agent is the loop, tools, permissions and context management around it. The model is what gets driven. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a harness"> The harness is the runtime around the model. The model contributes reasoning and nothing else. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a token"> A token is a unit of text. A model is the trained system that consumes and predicts tokens. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not inference"> Inference is the act of running a trained model. A model is the artefact that performs it. </Accordion>

Example

The published lineup makes selection concrete: Haiku at $1/$5 per million tokens for throughput-sensitive work, Opus for complex agentic coding, Fable for demanding long-horizon reasoning. Choosing between them is a decision made against published specs.

Related concepts

- Agent - the loop that drives a model
- Harness - the runtime around it
- Token - what it reads and writes

frontmatter.title: Observability
frontmatter.description: Instrumenting an AI system so you can see what it did in production - traces, token usage, tool calls and latency - and attribute failures to a cause.

body:
Definition
Instrumentation for an AI system in production: traces of what the model and tools did, token usage, latency, and cost attribution, so a failure can be diagnosed rather than guessed at.

Also known as
infrastructureobservabilitytracingmonitoringLLM tracing

Why it exists
An agent's output is the visible surface; its reasoning path is not. When a user gets a wrong answer you need to know which tool returned the bad data, which context was dropped, which model produced the claim - none of which the response contains. Observability supplies that missing middle.

How it works
Every API response reports what the request consumed in its usage field, which is the raw material for cost and token attribution. Around that, an agent needs a trace per run: the prompt assembled, each tool call with input and result, each model call with model id and token counts, and the final answer. Anthropic recommends recording which model id produced a result, since aliases move and only a pinned id tells you later whether behaviour changed because of the model.

Example
A support agent returns a wrong refund amount. The trace shows the tool call returned the right policy, but the context step had dropped the order history, so the model inferred the amount. Without the trace this is a model-quality bug you would try to fix with prompting.

When to use it
Instrument before you need it - there is no retroactive trace. Use it to answer which step produced a bad output, to attribute cost per feature, and to detect regressions between model versions. Do not log full prompt contents where the prompt contains user data or secrets without a plan.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Observability reconstructs **the middle** between prompt and answer: which tool returned what, which context was dropped, which model produced the claim.

Why it exists

An agent's output is the visible surface. Its path is not. When a user gets a wrong answer, the response tells you nothing about which tool returned bad data or which context was dropped - and both are far more likely causes than model intelligence.

How it works

The raw material exists already: every API response reports what the request consumed in its `usage` field, split into input, cache read, cache creation and output tokens. That gives you token and cost attribution per request for free.

Around it, a useful trace for one agent run contains:

- the prompt as assembled, including system prompt and tool definitions
- each tool call with its input and result
- each model call with its model id, token counts and latency
- the final answer, and any error or retry

 Record the **model id**, not the alias. Model aliases move to newer snapshots; only a pinned id tells you six months later whether a behaviour change came from the model or from your prompt. 

When to use it

Instrument before you need it - there is no retroactive trace. Use it to attribute a failure to a specific step, to attribute cost per feature or per tenant, and to catch regressions when a model snapshot changes underneath you.

Be deliberate about what you log. Traces contain prompts, which may contain user data. Decide the redaction and retention rules before you turn it on.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not an eval"> An eval measures quality against criteria and can gate a deploy. Observability records what happened in production. Both are needed. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not logging"> Logging emits strings for debugging. Observability needs a structured trace that reconstructs the decision path. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a guardrail"> A guardrail prevents or constrains behaviour. Observability measures and records it after the fact. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not token counting"> Token counting predicts input size before sending. Observability reports actual consumption from the usage field. </Accordion>

Example

A support agent returns a wrong refund amount. The trace shows the policy tool returned correct data, but the context step had dropped the order history, so the model inferred the amount. Without the trace this looks like a model-quality bug and you would try to fix it with prompting.

Related concepts

- Eval - quality gate before deploy
- Token - the unit you attribute cost in

frontmatter.title: Orchestration
frontmatter.description: The coordination layer that decides which agents, tools and models run, in what order, and with what isolation and context.

body:
Definition
The coordination layer that decides which agents, tools and models run, in what order, with what context isolation, and how their results combine.

Also known as
agentsmulti-agent orchestrationagent coordination

Why it exists
Once more than one agent or model is in play, the hard problem stops being 'can the model do the task' and becomes 'which worker gets which slice, with what context, and who merges the answers'. Orchestration names that problem so it can be designed instead of improvised.

How it works
Orchestration decides three things: assignment (which worker handles which slice), isolation (separate context window, separate git worktree, or shared), and aggregation (who merges results and how). Anthropic documents that dynamic workflows can choose which model an agent uses and whether subagents run in their own worktree. Claude Code additionally exposes parallel background session dispatch through agent view and the claude agents command.

Example
Ranking 80 resumes for a backend role: instead of one prompt, spawn pairwise comparison agents in a tournament bracket and merge the winners. Anthropic notes comparative judgement is more reliable than absolute scoring, and a deterministic loop holds the bracket while only the running order stays in context.

When to use it
Use orchestration when work splits into independent slices that benefit from clean context, when quality needs an adversarial second pass, or when items must be ranked and absolute scoring is unreliable. Do not orchestrate work that fits in one context window.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Orchestration is the coordination layer: **which worker gets which slice, with what context, and who merges the answers.**

Why it exists

One agent, one context window, one pass. That covers a lot. The moment work splits into independent slices, or needs a second opinion, or must rank hundreds of items, the bottleneck moves from the model's capability to the coordination design. Naming that layer makes it a design decision rather than something you rediscover every time.

How it works

Three decisions carry most of the weight.

**Assignment** - how work is divided. Classify-and-act routes by type; fan-out-and-synthesize sends one slice to each worker; tournaments have every worker attempt the same task so a judge can compare them pairwise.

**Isolation** - what each worker can see and touch. Anthropic notes dynamic workflows can decide whether subagents run in their own worktree, so a code fix can be developed in isolation and merged after review. Each worker also gets its own context window, which is the whole point: parallel work stops interfering.

**Aggregation** - how outputs become one answer. Anthropic is specific that the synthesize step is a barrier: it waits for all fan-out agents, then merges their structured outputs.

 Anthropic recommends keeping the deterministic part out of context. In a tournament, each comparison is its own agent, so the loop holds the bracket and only the running order stays in the context window. 

When to use it

Orchestrate when: work splits into slices that each benefit from a clean context; quality needs an adversarial verifier; or ranking many items is the task and pairwise comparison beats absolute scoring.

Do not orchestrate work that fits in one context window. Anthropic's warning is direct - dynamic workflows often use significantly more tokens and are best suited to complex, high-value tasks.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not a workflow"> A workflow is the predefined path. Orchestration is the coordination activity, which may follow a predefined path or not. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a harness"> The harness is the runtime. Orchestration is one policy that runtime executes. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a sub-agent"> A sub-agent is one worker. Orchestration decides whether to spawn it, what it gets, and where its output goes. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a tool"> A tool is one callable capability. Orchestration decides which capabilities run and in what sequence. </Accordion>

Example

Ranking 80 resumes for a backend role: spawn pairwise comparison agents in a tournament bracket, keep only winners, then double-check the top ten. Comparative judgement is more reliable than asking one agent to score 80 items against a rubric.

Related concepts

- Workflow - the predefined path orchestration may follow
- Harness - the runtime doing the coordinating
- Sub-agent - the worker that gets spawned

frontmatter.title: Plugin
frontmatter.description: A self-contained, shareable bundle of skills, agents, hooks and MCP server configuration for Claude Code.

body:
Definition
A self-contained directory, optionally with a .claude-plugin/plugin.json manifest, that bundles skills, agents, hooks and MCP server configuration so it can be installed, versioned and shared as one unit.

Also known as
mcppluginClaude Code pluginmarketplace plugin

Why it exists
Claude Code supports adding custom behaviour either standalone in .claude/ or as a plugin. Standalone is faster to iterate; plugins exist for the cases standalone cannot serve — sharing with teammates, distributing publicly, versioned releases, and reuse across projects. The plugin supplies identity and a namespace that a loose directory does not.

How it works
The manifest's name field is both a unique identifier and a namespace, so a bundled skill is invoked as /plugin-name:skill-name. Components inside skills/, agents/ and hooks/ are discovered automatically on install, and .mcp.json carries MCP server configuration. A plugin may hold a single component: a lone SKILL.md at the plugin root loads as one skill. Plugins install from a marketplace or a local directory via --plugin-dir.

Example
You have a code-review skill and a security-audit subagent that both need the same MCP server. Package them as one plugin: the manifest names it, the skills get the /acme-tools:code-review namespace, and a teammate installs everything with one command.

When to use it
Iterate standalone in .claude/ first, then convert to a plugin when you need to share it, version it, or reuse it across projects.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A Claude Code plugin is a self-contained directory — optionally with a `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` manifest — that bundles skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers and related components so they can be shared, versioned and installed as one unit.

Why it exists

Because there are two ways to add custom behaviour to Claude Code, and they suit different jobs. The official plugin guide puts it as a table:

ApproachSkill namesBest for
Standalone (`.claude/` directory)`/hello`Personal workflows, project customisation, quick experiments
Plugins`/plugin-name:hello`Sharing with teammates, distributing to the community, versioned releases, reusable across projects

The plugin is the answer to "how do I ship this to other people?" — it provides identity (name, description, version, author), a namespace for its skills, and an install path.

How it works

A plugin directory can contain:

text
`my-plugin/ ├── .claude-plugin/ │ └── plugin.json # manifest: name, description, version, author ├── skills/ # skills, namespaced as /my-plugin:skill-name ├── agents/ # custom subagents ├── hooks/ # event-triggered scripts └── .mcp.json # MCP server configuration`

The `name` in the manifest is both a unique identifier and a namespace — a skill in `my-plugin` is invoked as `/my-plugin:hello`. Skills, agents and hooks inside the plugin are discovered automatically on install. A plugin may contain just one component; the reference notes that a single `SKILL.md` at the plugin root is loaded as one skill.

Plugins install from a marketplace or from a local directory via `--plugin-dir`, which is how you test one before publishing it.

When to use it

Start standalone in `.claude/` while you are still iterating, then convert to a plugin when you need to share it, version it, or reuse it across projects. If nobody else will ever use it, a plugin is ceremony.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not an MCP server"> A plugin can *contain* MCP server configuration. That makes a plugin a superset of things, not a peer of one. The server is the program; the plugin is the box it ships in. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a skill"> A plugin is a container; a skill is one of the contents. A plugin with three skills is not a skill — it is a distribution unit holding three. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not an MCP connector"> A plugin is on disk before you install it. A connector is a live, configured connection afterwards. Shipping a plugin with `.mcp.json` describes what connecting it would do. </Accordion>

Example

You have built a `code-review` skill and a `security-audit` subagent that both need the same MCP server. Package them as one plugin: the manifest names it, the skills get the `/acme-tools:code-review` namespace, and a teammate installs the whole thing with one command and gets a consistent setup.

Related concepts

- Skill — one of the things a plugin bundles
- Sub-agent — another component type inside a plugin
- MCP connector — what a plugin's `.mcp.json` configures

title: Prompt injection
description: An attack where instructions hidden in content the model reads - a web page, a document, a tool result - override the task it was given.
summary: An attack where instructions hidden in content the model reads - a web page, a document, a tool result - override the task it was given.

frontmatter.title: Prompt injection
frontmatter.description: An attack where instructions hidden in content the model reads - a web page, a document, a tool result - override the task it was given.

body:
Definition
An attack in which instructions placed in content the model processes - a web page, an email, a document, a tool result - cause it to behave differently from its intended task, overriding the operator's instructions.

Also known as
safetyprompt injectionindirect prompt injectionLLM01

Why it exists
Agents read untrusted content as part of doing their job. The same channel that delivers the data delivers text, and the model has no reliable way to distinguish data from instructions. OWASP ranks prompt injection as LLM01:2025, the top risk in its GenAI list.

How it works
Direct injection is text the user types. Indirect injection is text embedded in something the agent fetches: a web page, a PDF, a code comment, an email, a tool response. OWASP notes the inputs need not be human-visible at all - as long as the content is parsed by the model, invisible characters can carry instructions. Critically, OWASP states that RAG and fine-tuning do not fully mitigate it.

Example
An agent asked to summarise a web page reads that page, which contains hidden text instructing it to send the conversation to an external URL. Because the agent has a fetch tool and credentials in context, the injected instruction can act. The defence is not better parsing - it is that the action requires approval.

When to use it
Treat any agent that reads untrusted content as exposed. Design for it from the start: least-privilege tools, human approval for irreversible actions, and no secret in the context that an injected instruction could exfiltrate. Do not rely on filtering the injection text as the primary defence.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Prompt injection is **instructions arriving through data**. The agent reads a page or a document for one reason and obeys text in it for another.

 OWASP ranks it LLM01:2025 - the top entry in its GenAI risk list - and states plainly that RAG and fine-tuning do not fully mitigate it. 

Why it exists

Because agents read untrusted content as part of the job. Web pages, tickets, PDFs, code comments, emails, tool results: all of them are data the agent must process, and all of them can carry text that reads as an instruction. The model has no reliable channel separation between the two.

How it works

**Direct** - a user types the instruction. That is the model doing what it was told.

**Indirect** - the instruction is embedded in content the agent fetches for another purpose. A web page, a document, a code comment, an email body, a tool response. This is the one that matters for agents.

Two properties from OWASP worth internalising:

- **It need not be visible.** The inputs can be imperceptible to humans; what matters is that

the model parses them. Invisible characters can carry instructions.

- **Famous mitigations do not close it.** OWASP states that techniques aimed at relevance and

accuracy - RAG, fine-tuning - do not fully mitigate prompt injection.

When to use it

Treat any agent that reads untrusted content as exposed, and design accordingly:

- Least privilege on tools. The agent should not be able to reach an action whose blast

radius matters without a human saying yes.

- Human approval for irreversible or outward-facing actions.
- No secrets in context that an injected instruction could exfiltrate through a tool.
- Treat retrieved documents as untrusted, whatever their source.

Do not make input filtering the primary defence. Filtering is one layer and it loses.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not a jailbreak"> A jailbreak is a user deliberately coaxing a model past its guidelines. Prompt injection reaches the model through content the agent reads for another reason. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not hallucination"> A hallucination is the model inventing false output with no attacker involved. Prompt injection is adversarial input causing changed behaviour. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not guardrails"> Guardrails are the defences. Prompt injection is the threat they mitigate. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not RAG"> RAG is a retrieval technique - and OWASP is explicit that it does not fully mitigate prompt injection, because retrieved text is another untrusted channel. </Accordion>

Example

An agent asked to summarise a web page reads that page, which contains hidden text telling it to send the conversation to an external URL. With a fetch tool and credentials in context, the injected instruction can act. The defence is not better parsing - it is that the action requires approval.

Related concepts

- Guardrails - the defences
- Agent - what the attacker is aiming at

body:
Definition
The input sent to a model for one turn - instructions, context and data. In an agent, the prompt is assembled by the harness each turn rather than written fresh by the user.

Also known as
promptingpromptsystem promptuser message

Why it exists
The model has no memory of prior turns other than what is resent. A prompt is the only channel through which instructions, retrieved documents and tool results reach it - so the shape and contents of that message are where most behaviour is decided.

How it works
A prompt is tokenised and prepended to the context. Anthropic's prompting guidance starts from a premise rather than a technique: define success criteria, have a way to test empirically, then improve the prompt. Its docs are explicit that not every failing eval should be solved by prompt engineering - latency and cost are often fixed more easily by choosing a different model.

Example
In an agent turn the 'prompt' is assembled: the system prompt, the conversation so far, tool definitions, retrieved context and the new user message. Writing the user message is a small part of it, which is why context engineering exists as a separate discipline.

When to use it
Use a prompt for success criteria you can control by wording - output format, tone, task framing, worked examples. Reach for a tool, a schema or a different model when the criterion is about capability rather than wording.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A prompt is the input for **one call**. In an agent, the harness assembles it every turn - so most of what you send is context you did not type.

Why it exists

The model has no memory beyond what is resent. Everything it knows about the task, the house rules and the documents arrives in that one message. The prompt is therefore the channel where almost all behaviour is decided.

How it works

Tokenised, then placed in the context alongside everything else. Anthropic's guidance is sequencing-shaped rather than technique-shaped: establish success criteria, build a way to test empirically, then iterate on the prompt against those criteria.

The important scoping note is from the same docs - this guide covers success criteria *controllable through prompt engineering*, and not every failing eval is best solved there. Latency and cost, Anthropic notes, are sometimes improved more easily by selecting a different model.

 The terms overlap in practice, so keep them distinct. The **system prompt** is the standing instruction block. The **user message** is this turn's request. The **full prompt** is everything: system prompt, history, tool definitions, retrieved context, new message. 

When to use it

Use the prompt for criteria you can move by wording: output shape, tone, framing, examples, constraints. Iterate on it when an eval fails and the failure is about behaviour you can describe.

Do not use it when the gap is capability. If the model cannot hold the reasoning chain, switching to a stronger model or giving it a tool beats rewording.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not prompting"> A prompt is the artefact. Prompting is the craft of deciding what goes in it and how to test whether it worked. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not the system prompt"> The system prompt is the standing instruction block. The user message is this turn's request. Only the latter changes per turn. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a skill"> A skill is packaged instructions reusable across tasks and loaded when relevant. A prompt is one assembled message for one call. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not context engineering"> A prompt is what you send. Context engineering is deciding, across a whole session, what should be in the window at each turn. </Accordion>

Example

An agent turn assembles a prompt from the system prompt, the conversation so far, the tool definitions, retrieved documents and the new user message. The user message is a small part of it - which is precisely why context engineering is a separate discipline from prompting.

frontmatter.title: Prompting
frontmatter.description: Writing and organising model instructions so the literal reading of your words produces what you intended.

body:
Definition
The practice of writing and organising the instructions given to a model so that reading them literally produces the intended behaviour, grounded in an explicit definition of success criteria.

Also known as
promptingprompt engineeringprompt designprompt

Why it exists
A model has no way to know what you want until you say so, and it reads what you say literally rather than charitably. Prompting is the discipline of making intent unambiguous enough that literal reading suffices. The official overview requires clear success criteria and a way to test empirically before any technique is worth applying.

How it works
Two factors decide whether a prompt works: clarity of the instruction, since vague output requirements produce varied output; and the success criteria behind it, since a prompt is only as good as the definition of good it was written against. The official guide covers criteria controllable through prompting, and notes that some failures are better fixed by a different model or latency choice.

Example
Weak: 'Summarise this document.' Stronger, because each clause removes a guess: 'Summarise this document in five bullet points. Use only information present in the document. If the document does not support a point, omit it rather than inferring one.'

When to use it
Every interaction involves prompting; the question is depth. Invest in prompt structure when the task repeats, when failure is expensive, or when output must be consistent. Keep it light for one-off exploration.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Prompting is the practice of writing and organising the instructions you give a model so it produces the behaviour you want — the deliberate shaping of one input artefact.

Why it exists

Because the model has no idea what you want until you say so, and it reads what you say literally rather than charitably. Prompting is the discipline of making your intent unambiguous enough that literal reading produces the intended result.

The official overview sets a precondition before any technique: have a clear definition of success criteria, some way to test empirically against them, and a first draft to improve. Technique without those is guesswork.

How it works

Two things determine whether a prompt works:

**Clarity of the instruction.** What the model reads is what it will do. Vague output requirements produce varied output.

**The success criteria behind it.** A prompt is only as good as the definition of "good" it was written against. This is why the evaluation documentation puts the two in a cycle: define criteria, build evaluations, improve, re-measure.

The official guide is also honest about scope. It covers success criteria "that are controllable through prompt engineering" — not every failure is a prompting failure. Sometimes a better model is the cheaper fix, and sometimes it is the only fix.

 Prompting optimises one artefact: the words you write. In a system that runs many turns with tools and retrieved data, the surrounding decisions dominate — that is context engineering. 

When to use it

Every interaction with a model involves prompting, so the question is not whether but how much. Invest in prompt structure when the task is repeated, when failure is expensive, or when the output must be consistent. Keep it light for one-off exploration.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not context engineering"> Prompting shapes the instruction text you write, once. Context engineering decides what else enters the window on every turn — tools, history, retrieved data — and is the binding constraint in multi-turn systems. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not evaluation"> A prompt is an input; an evaluation is the measurement of whether it worked. Writing a clever prompt with no way to tell whether it helped is the most common dead end in applied AI. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not fine-tuning"> Prompting changes behaviour by changing what you say at inference time. Fine-tuning changes weights. Prompting is cheaper, reversible and inspectable. </Accordion>

Example

Weak: "Summarise this document."

Stronger, because each clause removes a guess: "Summarise this document in five bullet points. Use only information present in the document. If the document does not support a point, omit it rather than inferring one."

title: RAG
description: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetching relevant passages at query time and putting them in the prompt, so answers come from current data.
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetching relevant passages at query time and putting them in the prompt, so answers come from current data.

frontmatter.title: RAG
frontmatter.description: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: fetching relevant passages at query time and putting them in the prompt, so answers come from current data.

body:
Definition
Retrieval-Augmented Generation - a technique that retrieves relevant passages from an external corpus at query time and appends them to the prompt, combining a model's parametric memory with non-parametric, revisable memory.

Also known as
retrievalRAGretrieval-augmented generation

Why it exists
Models store knowledge in parameters, which cannot be inspected, cited, or cheaply updated. RAG moves the knowledge out of the weights into a corpus the application controls, so answers can cite a source, knowledge can be revised without retraining, and provenance becomes available.

How it works
Offline, the corpus is chunked, each chunk is embedded into a vector, and the vectors are stored in a vector database. At query time, the query is embedded, the store returns the most similar chunks, and those chunks are appended to the prompt sent to the model. The original RAG paper frames this as combining pre-trained parametric and non-parametric memory for generation. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval work improves the retrieval step itself, reducing failed retrievals by 49%, and by 67% when combined with reranking.

Example
A support bot embeds the ticket, retrieves the five most similar past resolutions plus the current pricing policy, and appends them to the prompt. If the pricing changed last week, the fix is to reindex, not to retrain.

When to use it
Use RAG when the knowledge changes faster than you can retrain, when you need citations, or when the corpus is too large for the context window. Do not use it when the whole corpus fits - Anthropic notes that under roughly 200,000 tokens you can simply include the entire knowledge base in the prompt with no retrieval at all.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

RAG retrieves relevant passages at query time and puts them in the prompt, so the model answers from data you control rather than only from its weights.

Why it exists

Parametric memory - knowledge baked into weights - has three awkward properties: you cannot cite it, you cannot inspect what it actually contains, and updating it means retraining. RAG adds non-parametric memory: a corpus the application owns. The original paper is explicit that provenance and updating world knowledge were open problems that non-parametric memory addresses.

How it works

The pipeline has an offline half and an online half.

**Offline.** Break the corpus into chunks - typically no more than a few hundred tokens. Embed each chunk into a vector that encodes meaning. Store the vectors in a vector database that supports similarity search.

**Online.** Embed the query. The vector database returns the most similar chunks by semantic similarity. Those chunks are appended to the prompt sent to the generative model, which answers using them.

 The hard part is retrieval, not generation. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval work targets exactly this: it reduces failed retrievals by 49%, and by 67% when combined with reranking. An answer that would have been correct fails when the right passage was never retrieved. 

And the first question to ask is whether you need RAG at all. Anthropic notes that if the knowledge base is smaller than about 200,000 tokens - roughly 500 pages - you can include the whole thing in the prompt, with no retrieval layer at all.

When to use it

Use RAG when the knowledge changes faster than you can retrain, when you must cite sources, when the corpus exceeds the context window, or when different users need different corpora.

Do not reach for it on a small, static corpus. Retrieval adds a failure mode - the right passage not being retrieved - and a small corpus does not need one.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not fine-tuning"> Fine-tuning changes the weights. RAG leaves weights untouched and changes what is in the prompt at query time. RAG is cheaper to update and keeps sources inspectable. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not an embedding"> An embedding is the vector RAG uses to compare chunks. RAG is the whole system - chunk, embed, retrieve, augment, generate. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a vector database"> The vector database is the fast store inside the pipeline. RAG is the pipeline, and can use other retrieval mechanisms. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not MCP"> MCP is a protocol for connecting an AI app to systems. RAG is a technique for composing a prompt. An MCP server can serve documents to a RAG system, but RAG is not a connection protocol. </Accordion>

Example

A support bot embeds the ticket, retrieves the five most similar past resolutions plus the current pricing policy, appends them to the prompt, and cites them. When pricing changes last week the fix is to reindex the policy documents - not to retrain a model.

Related concepts

- Embedding - how chunks and queries become comparable
- Vector database - the store that makes retrieval fast
- Eval - how you know retrieval is working

frontmatter.title: Rate limits
frontmatter.description: Per-organisation caps on requests and tokens per minute, enforced with a token bucket, plus monthly spend limits your architecture must respect.

body:
Definition
Caps on how much an organisation may request per unit time - requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute - enforced with a token bucket, alongside monthly spend limits.

Also known as
fundamentalsrate limiting429throttlingquota

Why it exists
A provider serving many tenants has to bound peak load and prevent accidental overspend. The limits are therefore not an inconvenience but a contract your architecture must design around, because an agent multiplies request count per user request.

How it works
Limits are enforced at the organisation level and use a token bucket: capacity is continuously replenished up to the maximum rather than resetting on a fixed clock. Messages API limits are measured in requests per minute, input tokens per minute and output tokens per minute per model class. A breach returns HTTP 429 with a retry-after header indicating how long to wait. Spend limits separately cap monthly cost, and tier increases happen automatically as usage thresholds are reached.

Example
A fan-out workflow spawns twenty agents that each make ten tool calls. Without a queue you burst 200 requests and get a 429 mid-run; with a token-bucket-aware queue and retry-after handling the run completes, slower.

When to use it
Design for rate limits whenever an agent fans out - parallel subagents, fan-out workflows, batch classification. Do not serialise work that could safely be concurrent just to stay under a limit; queue and respect retry-after instead.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Rate limits are the **short-window throttle**: requests, input tokens and output tokens per minute, per organisation, enforced with a token bucket.

Why it exists

A provider serving many tenants has to bound peak load and prevent accidental overspend. That makes limits part of the contract your architecture designs around, not a surprise you handle after launch. An agent makes this worse by default: one user request can become twenty model calls.

How it works

**Token bucket, not a clock.** Capacity replenishes continuously up to the maximum instead of resetting at fixed intervals, so short bursts can exceed the nominal per-minute figure.

**Three separate meters.** Messages API limits are measured in requests per minute, input tokens per minute and output tokens per minute, per model class. You can be inside two of them and still get throttled on the third.

**The failure is legible.** A breach returns HTTP 429 with a `retry-after` header telling you how long to wait. That is enough to build correct backoff.

**A second ceiling exists.** Spend limits cap monthly cost independently of rate. Tiers increase automatically as usage thresholds are reached.

 The docs are specific that a limit of 60 requests per minute may be enforced as 1 request per second. Average-looking traffic can still be throttled, which is why backoff must read retry-after rather than retry on a fixed schedule. 

When to use it

Design for rate limits whenever an agent fans out - parallel subagents, fan-out-and-synthesize workflows, batch classification, tournament orchestration. Implement a queue and honour retry-after. Use the token counting endpoint to predict whether a batched request set will blow an input-tokens-per-minute meter before you send it.

Do not serialise work that could safely run concurrently in order to stay under a limit. That trades throughput for nothing.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not a token"> A token is the unit the limits are measured in. The rate limit is the cap. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not inference"> Inference is running a model. A rate limit throttles how much of that you may run per minute. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a spend limit"> Rate limits are the short window; spend limits are the monthly ceiling. Together they bound burstiness and total cost separately. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not the context window"> The context window caps one request's size. Rate limits cap how fast many requests arrive. </Accordion>

Example

A fan-out workflow spawns twenty agents making ten calls each. Unthrottled that is a 200-request burst and a 429 mid-run. With a token-bucket-aware queue honouring retry-after, the run completes - just slower.

Related concepts

- Token - what the limits meter
- API - the surface that returns 429

title: Skill (Agent Skill)

summary: A packaged instruction set — a SKILL.md directory — that teaches an agent a procedure and loads only when relevant.

frontmatter.title: Skill (Agent Skill)
frontmatter.description: A packaged instruction set — a SKILL.md directory — that teaches an agent a procedure and loads only when relevant.

body:
Definition
A directory containing a SKILL.md file with YAML frontmatter (required fields name and description) plus Markdown instructions, optionally with scripts, references and assets. It is loaded progressively: metadata always, the body when the task matches, supporting files only when referenced.

Also known as
mcpskillAgent SkillSKILL.md

Why it exists
Facts belong in CLAUDE.md; procedures do not. Procedures are long, only sometimes relevant, and loading them permanently wastes tokens on every unrelated conversation. Skills make procedural knowledge reusable without paying for it when it is not in play.

How it works
Agent Skills are an open standard at agentskills.io implemented by Claude Code. Required frontmatter is name (lowercase alphanumeric and hyphens, matching the directory) and description; license, compatibility, metadata and allowed-tools are optional. Progressive disclosure has three levels: frontmatter metadata is always in the system prompt, the SKILL.md body loads when the request matches the description, and linked scripts/references/assets load only when referenced. The description is what Claude matches against, so it must say both what the skill does and when to use it.

Example
A pdf-processing skill declares name and description in frontmatter and gives a three-step procedure in the body. Until someone asks about a PDF, only the two frontmatter lines occupy context — then Claude reads SKILL.md and runs scripts/fill_form.py rather than reasoning about PDF internals.

When to use it
When the gap is procedural knowledge you keep re-explaining — a house style, a release checklist, an analysis method, a document format. For access to a system, use an MCP server instead.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A Skill is a packaged set of instructions — a directory containing a `SKILL.md` file with YAML frontmatter plus Markdown — that teaches an agent how to handle a specific kind of task, loaded on demand rather than sitting in the context window permanently.

Why it exists

Because knowledge you want the model to *have* and knowledge you want it to *do something with* are different problems. Facts fit in `CLAUDE.md`. Procedures do not: they are long, they are only relevant sometimes, and loading them always wastes tokens on every conversation.

The official Claude Code guidance is explicit about the trigger — create a skill when you keep pasting the same instructions, checklist or multi-step procedure into chat, or when a section of `CLAUDE.md` has grown into a procedure rather than a fact.

How it works

Agent Skills are an **open standard**, documented at agentskills.io, and Claude Code implements it. The structure:

text
`skill-name/ ├── SKILL.md # required: frontmatter + instructions ├── scripts/ # optional: executable code ├── references/ # optional: documentation └── assets/ # optional: templates and resources`

Required frontmatter is two fields: `name` (lowercase, digits and hyphens, matching the directory name) and `description`. Everything else — `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata`, `allowed-tools` — is optional.

Loading is **progressive disclosure**, in three levels:

LevelWhat loadsWhen
1The `name` and `description` frontmatterAlways, in the system prompt
2The `SKILL.md` bodyWhen the task matches the description
3Linked files under `scripts/`, `references/`, `assets/`Only when referenced

Level 1 is the whole trick: the description is what Claude matches the user's request against to decide whether to load the skill at all, so it must state both what the skill does **and** when to use it. Because only the description occupies context until then, you can install many skills cheaply.

 This is the sharpest contrast with MCP. A skill adds *no new capability* — it cannot call your database. It changes how the agent uses the capabilities it already has. If you are reaching for a skill to grant access to a system, you want an MCP server. 

When to use it

Reach for a skill when the problem is procedural knowledge you keep re-explaining: a house style, a release checklist, an analysis method, a document format. Reach for an MCP server when the problem is access to a system.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not an MCP server"> A skill is prose and optional files on the agent's own filesystem. A server is a running process exposing callable capabilities over a protocol. A skill cannot be called; a server can. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a tool"> A tool has a name and an input schema and gets invoked. A skill has a description and Markdown and gets read. The presence of an input schema is the tell. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a plugin"> A skill is one component; a plugin is the packaging that ships it, with a manifest and a namespace. One plugin can hold many skills. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a prompt"> A prompt is a one-off instruction in a conversation. A skill is reusable, loads automatically when relevant, and can carry scripts and reference files with it. </Accordion>

Example

A PDF-processing skill:

markdown
`--- name: pdf-processing description: Extract PDF text, fill forms, merge documents. Use when handling PDF files or when the user mentions PDFs, forms, or document extraction. --- 1. Extract the page range you need first. 2. Use `scripts/fill_form.py` to fill the form; do not hand-edit PDF internals. 3. Verify the output opens before reporting success.`

Only the two frontmatter lines sit in context until someone asks about a PDF.

Related concepts

- Plugin — the package that ships skills
- Tool — a capability, unlike a skill's instructions
- Context engineering — why progressive disclosure matters

title: Structured Outputs
description: A decoding constraint that makes the model's response match your JSON Schema, so downstream parsing never fails.
summary: A decoding constraint that makes the model's response match your JSON Schema, so downstream parsing never fails.

frontmatter.title: Structured Outputs
frontmatter.description: A decoding constraint that makes the model's response match your JSON Schema, so downstream parsing never fails.

body:
Definition
A decoding constraint, configured via output_config.format with type json_schema, that forces the model's response to conform to a supplied JSON Schema. Paired with strict: true on tools, which guarantees tool names and inputs.

Also known as
promptingstructured outputsJSON outputsschema-constrained outputstrict tool use

Why it exists
Parsing untrusted model output is a recurring tax. The documentation lists malformed JSON, missing required fields, inconsistent types and schema violations as failure modes that occur even with careful prompting. Constraining decoding removes that failure class rather than reducing its probability.

How it works
You supply the schema in output_config.format with type json_schema, and the response text block conforms to it. The schema follows JSON Schema with documented limitations. The companion feature, strict tool use, applies the same guarantee to tool names and inputs. The two are independent and can be used separately or together.

Example
Sending a schema with required name, email and demo_requested and additionalProperties false guarantees the parser receives exactly those keys with those types — or you get an error at the API boundary instead of a runtime exception deep in your code.

When to use it
Whenever anything downstream parses the output — API responses, data extraction, tool inputs feeding code, anything writing to a database. The constraint costs little, since the model can still say whatever is true within the required shape.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Structured outputs are a decoding constraint that forces the model's response to conform to a JSON Schema you supply, so downstream code can parse it without defensive error handling.

Why it exists

Because parsing untrusted model output is a tax you pay on every request. The official documentation lists the failure modes without prompting: malformed JSON, missing required fields, inconsistent types, and schema violations that force retries.

Structured outputs removes that class of failure by constraining generation rather than asking nicely. The documented guarantees: always valid, type safe, and reliable — no retries needed for schema violations.

How it works

You send the schema in `output_config.format` with `type: "json_schema"`; the response comes back in the text content block already matching it. The schema follows JSON Schema, with some documented limitations.

The companion feature is **strict tool use** (`strict: true`), which applies the same guarantee to tool names and inputs. The documentation is explicit that the two are independent and can be used separately or together.

 This is a constraint on generation, not a test of truth. Structured output guarantees your parser will not crash. It guarantees nothing about whether the values inside are correct — that is the hallucination problem, and no schema can solve it. 

When to use it

Whenever anything downstream parses the output: API responses, data extraction, tool inputs feeding code, anything that writes to a database. The cost of the constraint is small — the model can still say whatever is true inside the required shape — so there is rarely a reason not to.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not a validation layer"> Post-hoc validation rejects bad output after generating it. Constrained decoding prevents invalid output from being generated. The former retries; the latter does not need to. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a correctness guarantee"> A schema-valid object can be entirely fabricated. Validity is syntactic; truth is semantic and must be verified separately. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a prompt"> A prompt asks the model to return JSON and it usually will. Structured output makes failure impossible by construction rather than probable by compliance. </Accordion>

Example

json
`"output_config": { "format": { "type": "json_schema", "schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "name": { "type": "string" }, "email": { "type": "string" }, "demo_requested": { "type": "boolean" } }, "required": ["name", "email", "demo_requested"], "additionalProperties": false } } }`

Your parser receives an object with exactly those keys and types — or you get an error at the API boundary instead of a runtime exception deep in your code.

Related concepts

- Hallucination — the problem this does not solve
- Tool calling — where strict tool use applies
- Prompting — the weaker alternative
