frontmatter.title: Sub-Agent
frontmatter.description: A delegated worker with its own context window, system prompt and tool access, returning a summary instead of a transcript.

body:
Definition
A specialised AI worker the main agent delegates a side task to. It runs in its own context window with its own system prompt and its own (often narrower) tool access, and returns a summary rather than its full transcript.

Also known as
agentssubagentsub-agentcustom subagentdelegated agent

Why it exists
Context preservation. The official guidance is to use one when a side task would flood the main conversation with search results, logs or file contents you will not reference again. The cost is not compute but context: every token of intermediate output is paid for twice, once occupying the window and once in what it displaced.

How it works
Each subagent gets its own context window, a focused system prompt, and its own tool access — restricting tools is how constraints get enforced, as with read-only exploration workers denied Write and Edit. Claude matches the subagent's description to decide when to delegate, which is why the official docs stress writing a clear description. A subagent works within a single session; parallel independent sessions are a separate surface in Claude Code.

Example
Asked why login is slow on staging, the answer may require reading six log files and three config files. A subagent reads all nine in its own window and returns three sentences; the main conversation never held the log text.

When to use it
When work is exploratory or bulky and its intermediate output will not be referenced again — codebase search, log analysis, reading many files. Also to constrain a task, since a review agent without a write tool cannot edit your code. Not for a two-step task you can simply do.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A sub-agent is a specialised AI worker that the main agent delegates a side task to; it runs in its own context window with its own system prompt and tool access, then returns a summary instead of its full transcript.

Why it exists

For context preservation. The Claude Code documentation gives the test directly: use a subagent when a side task "would flood your main conversation with search results, logs, or file contents you won't reference again."

That is a precise and unusual framing. The waste is not compute — it is *context*. You pay for every token of every search result twice: once while it sits in the main window crowding out what matters, and again in what it displaced.

A subagent turns that cost into a fixed one. The worker gets a fresh window, does its work, and the main conversation receives only the summary line.

How it works

Each subagent has:

- **Its own context window**, separate from the parent's.
- **Its own system prompt**, focused on one job.
- **Its own tool access**, which can be narrower than the parent's. Restricting tools is how

you enforce constraints — an Explore-style worker is read-only, with Write and Edit denied.

- **A description Claude matches against** to decide when to delegate. This is why the

official guidance repeats "write a clear description so Claude knows when to use it".

It runs within a single session. That boundary matters: for many independent sessions run in parallel, Claude Code offers a separate agent-view surface; for sessions that pass messages to each other, cross-session messaging; for coordinated teams, agent teams.

 A subagent is not a plugin component or an MCP server, even though a plugin can ship subagent definitions. The subagent is a running worker; the plugin is the packaging. 

When to use it

Use one when the work is exploratory or bulky and its intermediate output will not be referenced again: codebase searches, log analysis, reading many files, broad research. Also use one to *constrain* a task — a review agent with no Write tool cannot accidentally edit your code.

Do not use one for a two-step task you can just do. The subagent has real overhead: a new context, a summary round trip, and a summary that can lose detail you needed.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not an agent"> The agent is the loop that decides to delegate. The subagent is one delegated instance of that loop inside a single session. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a skill"> A skill is instructions the main agent reads and follows. A subagent is a separate worker with its own window that returns a result. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not an MCP server"> A server exposes capabilities; a subagent decides which of them to use. One subagent may call tools from three servers. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a plugin"> A plugin can package subagent definitions for distribution, but the subagent itself is a running worker, not a file on disk. </Accordion>

Example

Main conversation: "Why is login slow on staging?" — that answer may require reading six log files and three config files. A subagent reads all nine in its own window and returns three sentences. The main conversation never held the log text.

- Context engineering — why isolation matters
- Tool calling — what the subagent does inside its loop

frontmatter.title: Temperature
frontmatter.description: The sampling knob controlling how much randomness a model uses when picking the next token - and why the default is usually right.

body:
Definition
A sampling parameter that scales the randomness of next-token selection: low values make generation more deterministic and repetitive, high values more varied and more likely to drift.

Also known as
model-behaviortemperaturesampling temperaturetop_p

Why it exists
"Different tasks want different amounts of variation. A code edit should be

How it works
"The model produces a distribution over candidate next tokens. Temperature rescales

Example
"Two runs of a classification call at default temperature give slightly different

When to use it
"Leave temperature at its default for code, extraction, tool calls and anything

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Temperature scales **how random token selection is**. It controls variety, not quality, and not how much the model thinks.

Why it exists

Some tasks want reproducibility and some want variation, and the model should not have to guess which. Making it a parameter means the application decides, per call.

How it works

The model produces a distribution over candidate next tokens. Temperature rescales it before sampling:

- **Near zero** - the highest-probability token is almost always taken. Reproducible, and

repetitive.

- **Higher** - the distribution flattens, so rarer tokens are selected more often. Varied,

and more likely to drift off-target.

It is a sampling-time parameter applied per call. It does not change the model, and it does not change what the model knows.

 Temperature is not a reasoning control. If a task fails because the model did not think hard enough, the knob is thinking effort, a better prompt, a stronger model, or giving it a tool - not the sampling temperature. 

When to use it

Default for code, extraction, tool calls, and anything an eval gates on. Raise deliberately for creative drafting and brainstorming. Lower when you need the same answer twice.

Do not tune temperature to fix a hallucination or a logic error. Those are prompt, context, model or tool problems, and tuning the sampler makes the failure less predictable, not smaller.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not a model"> Temperature is a per-call sampling parameter applied at inference. It does not change or retrain the model. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a token"> Temperature changes how a token is selected. A token is the unit being selected. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not the prompt"> The prompt is the input. Temperature controls sampling while producing the output. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not thinking effort"> Effort controls how much reasoning happens before the answer, and costs output tokens. Temperature controls variety within the sampling. </Accordion>

Example

Two runs of a classification call at default temperature give slightly different wording. For a bug-report draft, higher temperature gives three genuinely different phrasings rather than three cosmetic variants of one.

- Model - what the parameter is applied to
- Eval - the gate that decides whether a change helped

frontmatter.title: Token
frontmatter.description: The unit a model reads and writes. Tokens are what context windows are measured in and what you are billed for.

body:
Definition
The unit of text a model processes and emits. Context windows are measured in tokens, billing is priced per million tokens, and rate limits are partly expressed as input and output tokens per minute.

Also known as
fundamentalstokenstoken countinput tokensoutput tokens

Why it exists
Text is not counted in characters or words by a model - it is counted in tokens. Every limit that matters (context window, cost, throughput) is denominated in tokens, so the token is the unit you must budget in.

How it works
The tokenizer splits text into tokens, which are embedded and processed. A token counting endpoint accepts the same structured inputs as the Messages API - system prompts, tools, images, PDFs - and returns the total input tokens before you send the request. Cached input is reported separately as input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens and cache_creation_input_tokens, and all three count toward the window. Counts are an estimate and may differ slightly; system-added tokens are not billed.

Example
Before a 200K-token window call, a count request tells you whether the assembled context fits. The docs are explicit that newer models use a different tokenizer: the same input text produces approximately 30 percent more tokens on Claude 4.7 and later than on earlier models, so a count measured against one model must not be reused for another.

When to use it
Count tokens before sending when you need to stay inside a rate limit, choose between models, or keep a prompt under a target length. Do not guess - tokenizer behaviour changes between model generations.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A token is the unit a model processes. Context windows are measured in them, price is per million of them, and rate limits are partly expressed as them per minute.

Why it exists

Because the model does not read characters. It reads tokens, and every constraint a product hits - window size, spend, throughput - arrives denominated in tokens. Budget in anything else and the arithmetic is wrong.

How it works

The tokenizer splits text into tokens which are embedded and processed by the model.

A counting endpoint exists precisely so you do not have to guess: it accepts the same structured inputs the Messages API does - system prompt, tools, images, PDFs - and returns the input token count before you send the real request.

Four details that change real numbers:

**Cached input is three fields, not one.** With prompt caching the input count splits into `input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens`, and all three count toward the context window.

**Counts are estimates.** The docs state the actual number used may differ by a small amount, so treat a count as a guardrail rather than an exact invoice.

**Tokenizers change between generations.** The docs note that Claude 4.7 and later use a newer tokenizer, producing approximately 30 percent more tokens for the same input text. A count measured on an earlier model is not transferable.

**Some inputs cannot be counted.** The endpoint returns an error for server tools such as web search and code execution, the MCP connector, and image or document blocks with a `url` or `file` source; send those as base64 to count them.

 Recount against the model you will actually use. Reusing a count measured on a previous generation is the single most common way people get surprised by an unexpected limit or bill. 

When to use it

Count before sending when you are near a rate limit, choosing between models, or holding a prompt to a length budget. Use it in CI as a guardrail that fails the build rather than discovering the overflow as a 429 at runtime.

Do not hand-count. Tokenizers are not intuitive and they change.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not the context window"> The context window is the capacity, measured in tokens. The token is the unit; the window is the limit. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a model"> A model consumes and predicts tokens. A token is one unit of that exchange. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a rate limit"> A rate limit caps requests or tokens per minute. The token is the unit that cap is measured in. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not context engineering"> Context engineering decides what goes into the window. Token counting measures the result of that decision, before the request. </Accordion>

Example

Assembling an agent context that you expect is near the limit, you call the counting endpoint with the same tool definitions you will send, and learn before the request that cached tool definitions plus the new user turn exceed the window you have left - then trim context rather than discovering a 400 at runtime.

Related concepts

- Context window - the capacity tokens are measured against
- Rate limits - per-minute caps denominated in tokens

title: Tool Calling

summary: The round trip in which a model requests a tool, your application executes it, and the result returns to the model.

frontmatter.title: Tool Calling
frontmatter.description: The round trip in which a model requests a tool, your application executes it, and the result returns to the model.

body:
Definition
The exchange in which a model decides a tool is needed and emits a structured request naming it with arguments, an application executes it, and the result is returned as a tool_result so the model can continue.

Also known as
agentstool usefunction callingtool_use

Why it exists
A model can only generate text. Tool calling is the explicit mechanism that turns generated text into an effect, and — equally important — into something checkable: the call is a structured object you can validate, log, gate or refuse before anything happens.

How it works
You send tool definitions; the API constructs a system prompt from them; the model returns a tool-use content block with a name and arguments; your application executes the call (client tools) or Anthropic does (server tools); you return the result in a tool_result block. Tool choice is driven by the pairing of the user's request with the tool description, which is why vague descriptions produce unreliable selection. An agent is what loops this until the task completes.

Example
The model emits tool_use(name='get_weather', input={'location': 'San Francisco, CA'}). Your code calls the weather API, gets 18 degrees and fog, and returns it as a tool_result. The model then writes the sentence the user reads. Only the first and last lines came from the model.

When to use it
When the task needs live or private data, or a side effect. Keep the tool set small and descriptions precise — every extra tool is another option the model might pick instead.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

Tool calling is the exchange in which a model decides a tool is needed, emits a structured request naming it and its arguments, your application executes it, and the result is fed back for the model to continue.

Why it exists

Because a model cannot act. It generates text. Tool calling is the narrow, explicit mechanism by which that text becomes an effect — and, just as importantly, by which it becomes *checkable*: the call is a structured object you can validate, log, gate or refuse before anything happens.

The official tool-use overview is precise about who does what: the model "returns a structured call that your application executes (client tools) or that Anthropic executes (server tools)."

How it works

Five steps, and step four is where applications go wrong:

- **Define** — send `tools` with each tool's name, description and `input_schema`.
- **Construct** — the API builds a system prompt from the tool definitions, telling the

model what is available.

- **Request** — the model returns a tool-use content block: the tool name plus arguments.
- **Execute** — *your application* runs it. For client tools this is entirely your code.
- **Return** — send the result back as a `tool_result` block; the model continues.

An agent is what loops steps 3 to 5 until the task is done.

The selection mechanism is the pairing of the user's request with the tool's description. That is why a vague description produces unreliable tool choice: the model has nothing else to go on.

 Two distinct things ride on the same word. A *client tool* is executed by your code. A *server tool*, such as web search, is executed by Anthropic. Over MCP, the server executes the tool and the client sends `tools/call` on its behalf. In all three cases the model only ever emits a request — it never runs anything itself. 

When to use it

Use tool calling when the task needs live or private data, or a side effect. Keep the tool set small and the descriptions precise: every extra tool is another option the model might pick instead of the one you wanted, and every ambiguous description is a coin flip.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not the tool definition"> The definition is the JSON you send. Tool calling is the round trip that follows. One definition, many calls. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not function execution"> The model never executes anything. It writes down a request. Your code decides whether to comply — that gap is where permissions, validation and safety live. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not the agent loop"> A single tool call is one exchange. The agent is the loop that repeats it, adds context and decides when to stop. </Accordion>

Example

text
`→ assistant: tool_use(name="get_weather", input={"location": "San Francisco, CA"}) ← your code: call the weather API, get 18°C and fog → you: tool_result(tool_use_id="...", content="18°C, fog") → assistant: "It's 18 degrees and foggy in San Francisco."`

The only part the model wrote was the first and last lines. The middle one was yours.

Related concepts

- Tool — the definition being called
- Agent — the loop that repeats the exchange
- MCP client — what executes the call over the protocol

summary: A single named capability a model can invoke — name, description and input schema — regardless of who defined it.

frontmatter.title: Tool
frontmatter.description: A single named capability a model can invoke — name, description and input schema — regardless of who defined it.

body:
Definition
A single named capability available for a model to invoke, defined by a name, a description of when to use it, and a JSON Schema for its input. Tools can be client tools you execute, server tools Anthropic executes, or tools exposed by an MCP server.

Also known as
mcptoolfunctiontool definitionfunction calling

Why it exists
A language model can only produce text. Tools are the mechanism that turns a generated sentence into an action — live lookups, private data, and real side effects. Without them an assistant can only describe how to do the thing.

How it works
A tool definition has a name matching ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$, a description covering what it does and when to use it, and an input_schema in JSON Schema. Claude chooses whether to call a tool from the user's request paired with that description. The model then returns a structured call request; your application executes it and sends the result back, and the model continues with the result in context. Over MCP the same shape appears as tools/list and tools/call.

Example
A get_weather tool with a location parameter: the model does not know today's weather, so it emits a structured call to get_weather with location 'San Francisco, CA', and your server performs the lookup and returns the result for the model to summarise.

When to use it
When the task needs information the model does not have, or an effect it cannot cause. Skip it when the answer is already in the prompt — a tool returning something you could have typed wastes a round trip.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A tool is a single named capability the model can invoke — a name, a description, and a schema for its input — whether it is defined by you in an API request, shipped by a vendor, or exposed by an MCP server.

Why it exists

A language model can only produce text. Tools are how it turns a sentence into an action: search a database, call an API, read a file, run a calculation. Without tools an assistant can tell you how to query your metrics; with them it queries them.

How it works

Three parts, and every one of them is load-bearing:

PartPurpose
`name`The identifier the model will emit. Must match `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$`
`description`What it does, **when it should be used**, and how it behaves
`input_schema`JSON Schema for the arguments

The description is doing more work than most people expect. Claude decides whether to call a tool based on the user's request and the tool's description — that pairing is the whole selection mechanism.

The round trip:

- You send the tool definitions with the request.
- The API builds a system prompt from them describing what is available.
- The model returns a structured request to call a tool, with arguments matching the schema.
- **Your application** executes it and sends the result back.
- The model continues, now with the result in context.

 Step 4 is the part people skip. On the Claude API, client tools are executed by your code, not by Anthropic. A model that "called your function" has done nothing yet — it has written down which function it would like called, and asked you to do it. 

Over MCP, the same shape appears at the protocol layer: a server returns tool definitions from `tools/list`, and a client sends `tools/call`. In that case the *client* executes on the server's behalf — but the model still only ever emits a request.

When to use it

Use a tool when the task requires information the model does not have, or an effect in the world it cannot cause: live data, private data, or a side effect. Do not use one when the answer is already in the prompt — a tool that returns something you could have just typed wastes a round trip and invites error.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not an MCP server"> A tool is one function inside a server. A server is the process that holds many tools plus resources and prompts. You almost never install a single tool; you install the server that carries it. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not an API endpoint"> A REST endpoint is a URL plus a method. A tool is a description of an intent plus a schema, designed for a model to choose. One endpoint can be exposed as one tool; one tool usually wraps a sequence of endpoint calls. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a skill"> A skill teaches; a tool acts. A skill changes what the model knows how to do procedurally; a tool gives it a new capability it can invoke. The clearest test: if it has an input schema, it is a tool. </Accordion>

Example

json
`{ "name": "get_weather", "description": "Get the current weather in a given location", "input_schema": { "type": "object", "properties": { "location": { "type": "string", "description": "The city and state, e.g. San Francisco, CA" }, "unit": { "type": "string", "enum": ["celsius", "fahrenheit"], "description": "The unit of temperature, either 'celsius' or 'fahrenheit'" } }, "required": ["location"] } }`

The model answers "What's the weather in San Francisco?" by emitting a call to `get_weather` with `location: "San Francisco, CA"`, and your code performs the lookup.

Related concepts

- Tool calling — the mechanism by which the model asks for it
- MCP server — the process that often exposes many tools
- Skill — instructions, not a callable capability

summary: Storage specialised for vectors that answers nearest-neighbour queries fast, so semantic search scales without comparing every pair.

frontmatter.title: Vector database
frontmatter.description: Storage specialised for vectors that answers nearest-neighbour queries fast, so semantic search scales without comparing every pair.

body:
Definition
Storage and indexing built for vectors that answers nearest-neighbour queries efficiently, so similarity search scales to millions of embeddings without an exhaustive pairwise comparison.

Also known as
retrievalvector storevector databasevector search

Why it exists
Comparing a query against every stored vector is O(n) per request. At a few thousand documents that is fine; at millions it is too slow and too expensive. A vector database indexes the space so only likely neighbours are examined.

How it works
Vectors are stored with an index - often an approximate nearest-neighbour structure such as HNSW or IVF - that narrows the search space. Exact search compares every vector; approximate search trades a little recall for a large speed gain. pgvector adds this to Postgres, supporting exact and approximate search over several distance metrics and vector types, so vectors live next to the rows they describe and keep ACID guarantees, JOINs and point-in-time recovery.

Example
Support articles and their ticket metadata live in one Postgres table with a vector column. Semantic search becomes a single indexed query that also filters by product and date - no second system, no synchronisation.

When to use it
Use a vector database when you have more than a few thousand embeddings and need semantic search over them, especially when the vectors should be joined with relational data. Stay on exact search, or plain brute-force comparison, while recall matters more than latency and the corpus is small.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A vector database stores embeddings and answers **nearest-neighbour queries fast**, so semantic search does not degrade into comparing every pair.

Why it exists

Brute-force similarity search is O(n). Fine for a few thousand chunks; unusable for millions, and the cost is per request. An approximate index narrows the space to likely neighbours, at the price of occasionally missing the true nearest one.

How it works

Vectors are stored alongside an index - commonly HNSW or IVF - that prunes the search space. Two settings you will meet:

- **Exact search** compares every vector. Highest recall, slowest.
- **Approximate search** uses the index. Large speedup, small recall cost.

pgvector implements both inside Postgres, across L2, inner product, cosine, L1, Hamming and Jaccard distance, and over single-precision, half-precision, binary and sparse vectors.

 The reason to pick Postgres-backed vectors over a dedicated store is usually not search quality - it is that the vector lives next to the row it describes. Filtering by product, tenant or date and ranking by similarity in one query removes an entire synchronisation problem. 

When to use it

Use one when the embedding count is large enough that brute force hurts, and especially when vectors must be joined with structured data. Use approximate search once recall is good enough; measure before you tune it.

Stay with brute-force exact comparison while the corpus is small enough that it is fast and recall is critical - approximate indexes on tiny datasets buy nothing.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not an embedding"> An embedding is the vector being stored. A vector database is the store and the index over those vectors. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not RAG"> RAG is the full pipeline, generation included. A vector database is the retrieval-side storage only. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a general database"> A relational database optimises for exact predicates and joins. A vector database optimises for similarity search, which is why the specialised index exists. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not an MCP server"> An MCP server exposes capabilities over the protocol. A vector database is a datastore your application queries directly. </Accordion>

Example

Support articles and their ticket metadata live in one Postgres table with a vector column. Semantic search is one indexed query that also filters by product and date - no second system and nothing to synchronise.

Related concepts

- Embedding - what it stores
- RAG - the pipeline it serves

title: Workflow

summary: An agentic system where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths, as opposed to a model that decides its own steps.

frontmatter.title: Workflow
frontmatter.description: An agentic system where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths, as opposed to a model that decides its own steps.

body:
Definition
An agentic system in which LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths written by a developer, rather than a model dynamically directing its own process and tool usage.

Also known as
agentsstatic workflowpredefined orchestration

Why it exists
Some tasks need the same reliable sequence every run - triage, extraction, a fixed review pipeline. A workflow makes the sequence explicit and inspectable, trading the flexibility of an open-ended agent for predictability and consistency.

How it works
The developer writes the control flow. LLM calls and tool calls are steps inside that flow, in a fixed order, with defined joins. Anthropic names the common patterns: prompt chaining, routing, parallelisation with an orchestrator step, and orchestrator-workers. Static workflows must handle every edge case, which is why Anthropic argues they are usually more generic than task-specific code.

Example
A support-ticket workflow is classify-then-route: score the ticket, route to the right queue, draft a reply from the queue's template, then emit a structured result. Four steps, always in that order.

When to use it
Use a workflow when the steps are known and well defined, when you need consistent and predictable behaviour, and when a failure should be attributable to a specific step. Use an agent instead when the path depends on what the model discovers.

Sourcing: verified

In one sentence

A workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through **predefined code paths**. The developer wrote the sequence; the model fills in the parts that need judgement.

Why it exists

An agent is given freedom, and freedom produces variance. When the sequence of steps is known in advance - triage this ticket, extract these fields, review this diff - writing it as code makes it inspectable, testable and repeatable. Anthropic's framing: workflows offer predictability and consistency for well-defined tasks, while agents are the better option when flexibility and model-driven decision-making are needed.

How it works

The control flow is yours. Anthropic names four patterns that recur:

- **Prompt chaining** - each step's output feeds the next, with validation gates between.
- **Routing** - a classifier step selects which specialised path to take.
- **Parallelisation** - independent subtasks fan out, then an orchestrator step aggregates.
- **Orchestrator-workers** - one LLM dynamically breaks the task down and delegates.

The important property is that the steps are fixed. Anthropic notes the tradeoff directly: static workflows need to work for every edge case, so they are usually more generic than you would write by hand for one task.

 Dynamic workflows blur this line. Claude Code can write a harness for itself on the fly - Anthropic documents this as dynamic workflows - which is closer to "the agent authors the workflow" than to a static one. The distinction that still holds: the code path is decided before or during the run, not discovered turn by turn. 

When to use it

Use a workflow when the steps are known, when you need consistent behaviour across runs, and when a wrong answer should be traceable to one step rather than to an opaque loop. Use an agent when the path depends on what the model finds.

Do not reach for a workflow when a single call with retrieval and in-context examples already solves the problem - Anthropic notes that for many applications, optimising single LLM calls is enough.

What it is not

<Accordion title="Not an agent"> An agent directs its own process and tool usage. A workflow follows paths the developer already wrote. This is the distinction Anthropic draws when splitting agentic systems into two categories. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a harness"> The harness is the runtime that executes the workflow. A workflow is a pattern the harness runs. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not orchestration"> Orchestration is the activity of coordinating agents, tools and models. A workflow is the specific predefined path that coordination follows. </Accordion>

<Accordion title="Not a skill"> A skill is packaged instructions describing a procedure. A workflow is executable structure

- control flow that actually runs.

</Accordion>

Example

A support-ticket workflow is classify-then-route: score the ticket, route it to the right queue, draft a reply from that queue's template, emit a structured result. Four steps, always in that order, and a failure points at one of them.

Related concepts

- Agent - the model-directed counterpart
- Harness - the runtime that runs a workflow
- Orchestration - coordination at runtime
